ticks.name: Recursive language
ticks.constraint: communication limited to immediate reality
ticks.detail: The ability to speak about things that don't exist — past, future, hypothetical, fictional. Other animals signal. Only sapiens narrate. Everything that follows — religion, law, science, money — is downstream of this.

links.label: Hauser, Chomsky & Fitch — The Faculty of Language (Science 2002)
Daniel Everett — Language: The Cultural Tool

ticks.name: Collective fiction
ticks.constraint: cooperation limited to kin groups (~150 people)
ticks.detail: Shared myths — gods, tribes, nations, money — let strangers cooperate at scale. Harari's central insight: intersubjective reality as the human superpower.

ticks.name: Cave painting / symbolic art
ticks.constraint: knowledge transfer limited to direct demonstration
ticks.detail: Chauvet, Lascaux, Altamira. External memory. The first medium. Art as knowledge storage before writing.

links.label: Nature: Oldest cave art found in Sulawesi

ticks.name: Burial ritual
ticks.constraint: death as a purely physical event
ticks.detail: The first evidence of deliberate burial with grave goods implies belief in an afterlife. The tick that made religion — and therefore civilization — possible.

links.label: Shanidar Cave and Neanderthal burial debate
Paul Pettitt — Palaeolithic Origins of Human Burial

ticks.name: Bone flute / intentional music
ticks.constraint: sound as functional signal only
ticks.detail: Music binds groups emotionally, synchronizes bodies, creates shared identity. A social technology before the word existed.

links.label: Nature: Bone flutes and the origins of music
Music and the evolution of human sociality

ticks.name: Wheat domestication
ticks.constraint: food supply as contingent on movement
ticks.detail: Surplus food enabled permanent settlement — and with it, hierarchy, specialization, writing, cities, armies.

links.label: Science: Genome of wild emmer wheat
Jared Diamond — Guns, Germs and Steel (Ch. 5)

ticks.name: Animal domestication
ticks.constraint: protein requiring active hunting
ticks.detail: Each domesticated species was its own tick. Also brought zoonotic disease, which devastated unexposed populations for millennia.

links.label: PNAS: Worldwide patterns of livestock domestication
Jared Diamond — Guns, Germs and Steel

ticks.name: Pottery / fired clay
ticks.constraint: food storage limited to immediate consumption
ticks.detail: Grain in storage is the first treasury.

links.label: Smithsonian: World's oldest pottery found in China
Pottery and the storage revolution — archaeology review

ticks.name: Irrigation canals
ticks.constraint: farming limited to rainfall patterns
ticks.detail: Also unlocked the first bureaucracies — someone had to manage water rights.

links.label: PNAS: Irrigation and early state formation

ticks.name: Fermentation (beer and bread)
ticks.constraint: grain as perishable raw material
ticks.detail: Beer was currency, ration, and social glue in early Mesopotamia. Fermentation is biotechnology's first application.

links.label: Nature: Chemical evidence of earliest beer brewing

ticks.name: Loom weaving
ticks.constraint: fabric production requiring hand-knotting
ticks.detail: Textile trade was the engine of the ancient economy.

ticks.name: The wheel
ticks.constraint: load transport requiring human or animal carrying
ticks.detail: A cart pulled by an ox moves ten times more goods than a person carrying.

ticks.name: Cuneiform writing
ticks.constraint: memory and record limited to what a human brain holds
ticks.detail: Writing began as a spreadsheet, not a story.

links.label: Andrew Robinson — The Story of Writing

ticks.name: Trepanation (skull drilling)
ticks.constraint: the skull as inviolable and impenetrable
ticks.detail: Evidence of skull drilling with stone tools found across multiple continents — and many patients survived. The oldest known surgical procedure.

ticks.name: Egyptian hieroglyphics (phonetic principle)
ticks.constraint: writing as pure logography
ticks.detail: The phonetic turn made writing learnable by more people and adaptable to new words.

ticks.name: Double-entry bookkeeping
ticks.constraint: trust in economic exchange
ticks.detail: Made commerce legible and auditable without requiring trust in individuals.

ticks.name: City-state governance
ticks.constraint: social order requiring personal authority of a known leader
ticks.detail: Law as a system rather than a ruler's whim.

ticks.name: Pyramid construction
ticks.constraint: monumental architecture as impossible for human labor
ticks.detail: A proof of concept for state power.

ticks.name: Akkadian Empire (first empire)
ticks.constraint: political order limited to a single city or valley
ticks.detail: The first empire. With it: standardized weights, unified law, and tribute systems.

ticks.name: Babylonian quadratic equations
ticks.constraint: equations requiring geometric intuition to solve
ticks.detail: Mathematics as repeatable algorithmic process, not just measurement.

ticks.name: Code of Hammurabi
ticks.constraint: justice as personal and arbitrary
ticks.detail: The principle that law should be knowable in advance is civilization's operating system.

links.label: Louvre Museum: The Code of Hammurabi stele
Full text of Hammurabi's Code — Yale Avalon Project

ticks.name: Alphabetic writing (Phoenician)
ticks.constraint: writing requiring years of specialist training
ticks.detail: Every alphabet in use today traces to the Phoenicians.

links.label: Smithsonian: The alphabet that changed the world
John Man — Alpha Beta: How 26 Letters Shaped the Western World

ticks.name: Monotheism (Akhenaten)
ticks.constraint: divine power as distributed among competing gods
ticks.detail: Seeded Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

ticks.name: Silk Road trade routes
ticks.constraint: luxury goods as locally constrained
ticks.detail: Buddhism reached China; the Black Death reached Europe along the same routes.

links.label: Google Scholar: Silk Road trade routes

ticks.name: Iron smelting
ticks.constraint: metal tools limited by bronze's rare ingredient (tin)
ticks.detail: The Bronze Age collapse was partly iron-armed raiders disrupting palace economies.

ticks.name: Greek alphabet with vowels
ticks.constraint: reading requiring contextual knowledge to decode
ticks.detail: Literacy became teachable to anyone. Greece's philosophical explosion follows directly.

links.label: Google Scholar: Greek alphabet with vowels

ticks.name: Coined money (Lydia)
ticks.constraint: trade requiring barter or weighing commodity metals
ticks.detail: Coinage enabled markets, armies, and taxation at scales impossible before.

ticks.name: Pre-Socratic natural philosophy
ticks.constraint: natural phenomena requiring divine explanation
ticks.detail: Nature can be explained without gods, and this explanation can be argued about.

ticks.name: Buddhism (Four Noble Truths)
ticks.constraint: suffering as imposed by gods or fate
ticks.detail: Still the most rigorous pre-modern framework for mind science.

ticks.name: Confucianism
ticks.constraint: social order requiring divine mandate or force
ticks.detail: Two thousand years of Chinese governance runs on this operating system.

ticks.name: Pāṇini's Sanskrit grammar
ticks.constraint: language as describable only by example, not rule
ticks.detail: The first formal generative grammar in human history — 2,400 years before Chomsky.

ticks.name: Athenian democracy
ticks.constraint: legitimate political authority requiring hereditary or divine origin
ticks.detail: Every modern democracy traces its vocabulary to Athens.

ticks.name: Socratic method
ticks.constraint: knowledge as received from authority
ticks.detail: Every scientific debate and legal cross-examination descends from this.

ticks.name: Sushruta Samhita (surgical manual)
ticks.constraint: surgery as ad-hoc and untransmissible
ticks.detail: Described 300 surgical procedures. The first systematic surgical textbook. Described hand-washing 2,400 years before Semmelweis.

ticks.name: Aristotle's formal logic
ticks.constraint: argument as purely rhetorical
ticks.detail: Foundation of mathematics, law, computer science, and every field requiring rigorous proof.

links.label: Aristotle — Prior Analytics — Internet Classics Archive
Jonathan Lear — Aristotle and Logical Theory

ticks.name: Euclid's Elements
ticks.constraint: mathematical truth as empirical or approximate
ticks.detail: The first closed deductive system. Still used to teach proof.

ticks.name: Heliocentric model (Aristarchus)
ticks.constraint: Earth as center of the universe
ticks.detail: The tick happened twice: the idea was right but the instruments weren't ready.

ticks.name: Archimedes / statics and buoyancy
ticks.constraint: physical phenomena as describable only qualitatively
ticks.detail: Mathematics applied to physical forces. The first quantitative physics.

links.label: Google Scholar: Archimedes / statics and buoyancy

ticks.name: Roman roads
ticks.constraint: army movement speed limited by terrain
ticks.detail: The same infrastructure accelerated trade, communication, and disease spread.

ticks.name: Codex format (bound pages)
ticks.constraint: text requiring sequential reading from a scroll
ticks.detail: The book as random-access storage. A format that dominated for 1,500 years.

ticks.name: Rosetta Stone / parallel text decipherment
ticks.constraint: ancient scripts as permanently undecipherable
ticks.detail: Champollion's 1822 decipherment unlocked hieroglyphics. The method became the template for deciphering all lost scripts.

links.label: Wikipedia: Rosetta Stone / parallel text decipherment
Google Scholar: Rosetta Stone / parallel text decipherment

ticks.name: Ptolemy's coordinate system
ticks.constraint: maps as schematic and non-projectable
ticks.detail: Every map since uses his coordinate system.

ticks.name: Paper (Cai Lun, Han Dynasty)
ticks.constraint: writing requiring expensive or heavy materials
ticks.detail: China's administrative sophistication was built on paper.

links.label: Google Scholar: Paper (Cai Lun, Han Dynasty)

ticks.name: Symbolic algebra notation (Diophantus)
ticks.constraint: equations requiring full verbal description
ticks.detail: Notation is cognition: the symbol system determines what problems you can even think about.

ticks.name: Christianity as state religion
ticks.constraint: empire requiring polytheistic accommodation
ticks.detail: The most durable administrative structure in Western history.

links.label: Google Scholar: Christianity as state religion

ticks.name: Islam / the Quran
ticks.constraint: Arab tribal fragmentation
ticks.detail: The Quran as constitution, law code, and scripture simultaneously.

ticks.name: Arabic numerals and zero
ticks.constraint: arithmetic impossible with Roman numeral system
ticks.detail: The numeral system is a cognitive prosthetic.

links.label: Google Scholar: Arabic numerals and zero

ticks.name: Algebra (al-Khwarizmi)
ticks.constraint: equations solvable only case-by-case
ticks.detail: Every variable in every equation since traces here.

ticks.name: First printed book (Diamond Sutra)
ticks.constraint: book production as always hand-copied
ticks.detail: Woodblock printing preceded Gutenberg by 600 years.

links.label: Google Scholar: First printed book (Diamond Sutra)

ticks.name: Canon of Medicine (Avicenna)
ticks.constraint: medicine as tradition-bound and unsystematic
ticks.detail: Introduced clinical trials and quarantine. Primary medical textbook in Europe until the 17th century.

ticks.name: Optics and experiment (Ibn al-Haytham)
ticks.constraint: vision as the eye projecting light outward
ticks.detail: First documented use of controlled experiments in natural science.

links.label: Google Scholar: Optics and experiment (Ibn al-Haytham)

ticks.name: Musical staff notation (Guido d'Arezzo)
ticks.constraint: music transmission requiring memorization
ticks.detail: Composition became separable from performance. Polyphony and classical music require this tick.

links.label: Google Scholar: Musical staff notation (Guido d'Arezzo)

ticks.name: University as institution
ticks.constraint: advanced knowledge requiring monastic or court patronage
ticks.detail: The corporate structure that lets knowledge accumulate across generations. We still use the model.

ticks.name: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci
ticks.constraint: European commerce using Roman numerals
ticks.detail: The book that made capitalism computationally possible.

ticks.name: Magna Carta
ticks.constraint: royal authority as unlimited
ticks.detail: Every constitution inherits this idea.

links.label: British Library: Magna Carta — history and significance

ticks.name: Eyeglasses
ticks.constraint: presbyopia as the end of intellectual productivity
ticks.detail: The intellectual workforce effectively doubled its productive years.

ticks.name: Mechanical clock
ticks.constraint: time as natural and approximate
ticks.detail: Time as a managed resource rather than a natural flow.

ticks.name: Black Death as social disruptor
ticks.constraint: feudal labor relations (by killing a third of Europe)
ticks.detail: Surviving peasants had leverage. Wages rose. The economic disruption forced transitions that led to the Renaissance.

links.label: Wikipedia: Black Death as social disruptor
Google Scholar: Black Death as social disruptor

ticks.name: Linear perspective (Brunelleschi)
ticks.constraint: depicted space as symbolic and flat
ticks.detail: Painting became a science of vision. Also unlocked engineering drawing.

ticks.name: Brunelleschi's dome (Florence)
ticks.constraint: large dome construction requiring wooden centering
ticks.detail: The Renaissance begins in this dome.

ticks.name: Gutenberg's printing press
ticks.constraint: text reproduction requiring manual copying
ticks.detail: The Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and mass literacy all follow.

links.label: Elizabeth Eisenstein — The Printing Press as an Agent of Change

ticks.name: Columbian Exchange
ticks.constraint: Old and New World as biologically separate
ticks.detail: The largest ecological event since the ice age.

ticks.name: Ambroise Paré / wound treatment reform
ticks.constraint: gunshot wounds requiring boiling oil cauterization
ticks.detail: Evidence-based surgery before the term existed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Ambroise Paré / wound treatment reform
Google Scholar: Ambroise Paré / wound treatment reform

ticks.name: Copernican heliocentrism
ticks.constraint: human civilization as the cosmic center
ticks.detail: The first crack in the theological worldview that structured medieval Europe.

links.label: Dava Sobel — A More Perfect Heaven

ticks.name: Human anatomy (Vesalius)
ticks.constraint: the body as known through Galen's ancient texts
ticks.detail: The body is knowable through direct observation, not authority.

ticks.name: Mercator projection
ticks.constraint: compass bearing requiring curved-surface math
ticks.detail: Navigators could plot courses by drawing straight lines.

ticks.name: Dutch East India Company (first joint-stock co.)
ticks.constraint: large ventures limited by single investor's capital
ticks.detail: The corporation as a legal structure unlocked capitalism's scaling mechanism.

links.label: Femme Gaastra — The Dutch East India Company
William Bernstein — The Birth of Plenty

ticks.name: Amsterdam Stock Exchange
ticks.constraint: investment requiring direct relationship with issuer
ticks.detail: Secondary market trading — buying and selling existing shares — was born.

ticks.name: Compound microscope
ticks.constraint: the visible as the limit of the knowable
ticks.detail: An entire scale of reality no one had ever seen.

ticks.name: Experimental method (Bacon)
ticks.constraint: knowledge as derived from ancient authority or pure reason
ticks.detail: The philosophical foundation of modern science.

ticks.name: Equal temperament tuning
ticks.constraint: instruments out of tune across keys
ticks.detail: Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier. The Western classical tradition requires this tick.

ticks.name: Telescope as scientific instrument (Galileo)
ticks.constraint: astronomical knowledge as naked-eye observation
ticks.detail: Instruments could reveal what no human had ever seen.

links.label: Google Scholar: Telescope as scientific instrument (Galileo)

ticks.name: Logarithms (Napier)
ticks.constraint: multiplication of large numbers as hours of calculation
ticks.detail: Log tables convert multiplication into addition.

ticks.name: First sign language alphabet (Juan Pablo Bonet)
ticks.constraint: deaf people as unable to communicate in formal settings
ticks.detail: The foundation of what became modern signed languages.

links.label: Wikipedia: First sign language alphabet (Juan Pablo Bonet)
Google Scholar: First sign language alphabet (Juan Pablo Bonet)

ticks.name: Blood circulation (Harvey)
ticks.constraint: blood as consumed by organs rather than circulating
ticks.detail: First mathematical proof in medicine. The body as a hydraulic system.

ticks.name: Cartesian coordinates (Descartes)
ticks.constraint: algebra and geometry as separate disciplines
ticks.detail: Every graph, every data visualization, every physics simulation uses this framework.

ticks.name: Tulip mania (first speculative bubble)
ticks.constraint: market prices as tethered to intrinsic value
ticks.detail: The first documented speculative bubble proved market prices can disconnect entirely from underlying value.

links.label: Google Scholar: Tulip mania (first speculative bubble)

ticks.name: Probability theory (Pascal/Fermat)
ticks.constraint: uncertain future outcomes as unquantifiable
ticks.detail: Insurance, statistics, financial derivatives, ML — all require a mathematics of uncertainty.

ticks.name: The Sceptical Chymist (Boyle)
ticks.constraint: matter as composed of four classical elements
ticks.detail: Chemistry could not become a science until it abandoned ancient element theory.

ticks.name: Cell theory (Hooke / Leeuwenhoek)
ticks.constraint: life as having no structural unit
ticks.detail: Everything else (cancer, infection, development, evolution) is a story about cells.

ticks.name: Newton's Principia / universal gravitation
ticks.constraint: earthly and celestial physics as separate domains
ticks.detail: One mathematical law describes both. The confidence that nature has laws begins here.

links.label: Richard Westfall — Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton

ticks.name: Lloyds of London (insurance market)
ticks.constraint: maritime risk as borne entirely by ship owners
ticks.detail: Risk-sharing as a market mechanism unlocked global trade at scales individual risk tolerance could never support.

links.label: Google Scholar: Lloyds of London (insurance market)

ticks.name: Bank of England (central bank concept)
ticks.constraint: government financing as dependent on individual lenders
ticks.detail: Every central bank (Fed, ECB, RBI) is a variation on this model.

links.label: Wikipedia: Bank of England (central bank concept)
Google Scholar: Bank of England (central bank concept)

ticks.name: First daily newspaper (Daily Courant)
ticks.constraint: public information as irregular and rumor-based
ticks.detail: Public opinion as a force — and the possibility of propaganda — both require mass daily news.

links.label: Google Scholar: First daily newspaper (Daily Courant)

ticks.name: Copyright law (Statute of Anne)
ticks.constraint: authors' works as property of printers indefinitely
ticks.detail: Every IP law, patent system, and creator economy descends from this statute.

links.label: Google Scholar: Copyright law (Statute of Anne)

ticks.name: Graph theory (Euler / Königsberg bridges)
ticks.constraint: network problems as geometric rather than topological
ticks.detail: Now underlies social networks, the internet's routing, supply chains, and the structure of the human brain.

links.label: Google Scholar: Graph theory (Euler / Königsberg bridges)

ticks.name: Separation of powers (Montesquieu)
ticks.constraint: government as unified under a single authority
ticks.detail: The US Constitution, and every liberal democracy's structure, is an implementation of this idea.

ticks.name: L'Épée's school / French Sign Language
ticks.constraint: deaf education as impossible
ticks.detail: His students emigrated to the US and seeded American Sign Language.

links.label: Wikipedia: L'Épée's school / French Sign Language
Google Scholar: L'Épée's school / French Sign Language

ticks.name: Marine chronometer (Harrison)
ticks.constraint: longitude at sea as uncomputable
ticks.detail: Harrison ended the problem that had killed thousands of sailors.

ticks.name: Social contract theory (Rousseau)
ticks.constraint: political authority as derived from God or tradition
ticks.detail: The French and American revolutions are implementations of this idea.

ticks.name: Oxygen (Priestley/Lavoisier)
ticks.constraint: combustion as releasing phlogiston
ticks.detail: Modern chemistry — stoichiometry, conservation of mass, the periodic table — begins here.

ticks.name: Wealth of Nations (Adam Smith)
ticks.constraint: wealth as a fixed quantity nations compete over
ticks.detail: Every free market economy is an experiment in this hypothesis.

links.label: Google Scholar: Wealth of Nations (Adam Smith)

ticks.name: Comparative linguistics (Sir William Jones)
ticks.constraint: languages as unrelated products of separate civilizations
ticks.detail: Founded historical comparative linguistics. English, Hindi, Farsi, and Greek are cousins.

links.label: Google Scholar: Comparative linguistics (Sir William Jones)

ticks.name: Buttonwood Agreement (NYSE founding)
ticks.constraint: US securities trading as informal and fraud-prone
ticks.detail: The formalization of rules that made securities markets reliable.

ticks.name: Steam engine (Watt's rotary motion)
ticks.constraint: mechanical power limited to water, wind, and muscle
ticks.detail: The energy transition from organic to fossil fuel.

links.label: Google Scholar: Steam engine (Watt's rotary motion)

ticks.name: Galvani / bioelectricity
ticks.constraint: nerve impulse as mechanical rather than electrical
ticks.detail: Every neuroscience discovery, every brain-computer interface, every EEG and MRI traces to this tick.

ticks.name: Vaccination (Jenner)
ticks.constraint: immunity requiring natural infection
ticks.detail: The tick that eventually eradicated smallpox and is currently eliminating polio.

links.label: Jenner — An Inquiry into Causes of Variolae Vaccinae (1798)

ticks.name: Voltaic pile (first battery)
ticks.constraint: electricity as a static phenomenon requiring friction
ticks.detail: Electricity became controllable. Enabled electrolysis, electroplating, the telegraph.

ticks.name: Abolition of the slave trade (Britain)
ticks.constraint: the legal personhood of humans as purchasable
ticks.detail: A template for all subsequent human rights legislation.

links.label: Wikipedia: Abolition of the slave trade (Britain)
Google Scholar: Abolition of the slave trade (Britain)

ticks.name: Proto-Indo-European reconstruction (Bopp)
ticks.constraint: ancient extinct languages as permanently unknowable
ticks.detail: Historical linguistics as a rigorous science.

ticks.name: Anesthesia / ether
ticks.constraint: surgery limited by the patient's ability to endure pain
ticks.detail: Modern surgery begins here.

ticks.name: Penny press (mass-market newspaper)
ticks.constraint: newspapers affordable only by the wealthy
ticks.detail: The advertising-supported media model that still dominates begins here.

ticks.name: Photography (Daguerre)
ticks.constraint: visual record requiring an artist's interpretation
ticks.detail: Also freed painting from the obligation to represent.

ticks.name: First public surgery under ether (Morton)
ticks.constraint: the operating theater as a theater of screaming
ticks.detail: Within months, ether was used in operating rooms across Europe.

links.label: Wikipedia: First public surgery under ether (Morton)
Google Scholar: First public surgery under ether (Morton)

ticks.name: Communist Manifesto (Marx/Engels)
ticks.constraint: economic relations as natural rather than political
ticks.detail: The next century of political history is a response to this document.

ticks.name: Chicago Board of Trade (commodity futures)
ticks.constraint: grain farmers' revenue as unpredictable until harvest
ticks.detail: Futures markets decoupled price discovery from physical delivery.

links.label: Wikipedia: Chicago Board of Trade (commodity futures)
Google Scholar: Chicago Board of Trade (commodity futures)

ticks.name: Phineas Gage / frontal lobe case
ticks.constraint: personality as separate from brain structure
ticks.detail: Personality, social behavior, and decision-making are produced by specific brain regions.

links.label: Wikipedia: Phineas Gage / frontal lobe case
Google Scholar: Phineas Gage / frontal lobe case

ticks.name: Elevator safety brake (Otis)
ticks.constraint: building height limited by stair-climbing practicality
ticks.detail: The skyscraper, the vertical city, and urban density all become possible.

ticks.name: Boolean algebra (Boole)
ticks.constraint: logic as verbal and informal
ticks.detail: Every computer processor is Boolean algebra made physical.

ticks.name: Synthetic dye (Perkin's mauveine)
ticks.constraint: color requiring rare organic sources
ticks.detail: The chemical industry as a separate industry begins here.

ticks.name: On the Origin of Species (Darwin)
ticks.constraint: species as fixed and divinely created
ticks.detail: The most destabilizing scientific idea in history.

links.label: Darwin — On the Origin of Species (1859) — full text
Wikipedia: On the Origin of Species
Janet Browne — Charles Darwin: A Biography

ticks.name: Broca's area (language localization)
ticks.constraint: brain as homogeneous and non-localized
ticks.detail: The brain has specific regions for specific functions. Neuroimaging begins with this discovery.

ticks.name: Germ theory (Pasteur/Koch)
ticks.constraint: disease as caused by miasma or internal imbalance
ticks.detail: Life expectancy doubled in the century after this tick.

links.label: John Waller — The Discovery of the Germ

ticks.name: Manet / Salon des Refusés
ticks.constraint: painting as requiring idealized or historically justified subjects
ticks.detail: Impressionism, modernism, and the avant-garde all begin here.

links.label: Google Scholar: Manet / Salon des Refusés

ticks.name: Geneva Convention
ticks.constraint: war as having no rules for treatment of the wounded
ticks.detail: The tick that war itself has legal constraints binding on all parties.

ticks.name: Antiseptic surgery (Lister)
ticks.constraint: surgical infection as inevitable and mysterious
ticks.detail: Post-surgical mortality dropped from ~50% to ~15% almost immediately.

links.label: Lister — On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery (1867)
Fitzharris — The Butchering Art (biography of Lister)

ticks.name: Periodic table (Mendeleev)
ticks.constraint: elements as unrelated individuals
ticks.detail: Chemistry became a predictive science.

ticks.name: Set theory (Cantor)
ticks.constraint: infinity as a single undifferentiated concept
ticks.detail: Some infinities are larger than others. Foundation of all mathematics.

ticks.name: Telephone (Bell)
ticks.constraint: voice communication requiring physical proximity
ticks.detail: Restructured social space as completely as roads restructured physical space.

ticks.name: Phonograph (Edison)
ticks.constraint: music as existing only in the moment of performance
ticks.detail: The entire recorded music industry, radio, and streaming descend from this tick.

ticks.name: Electric light (Edison's grid system)
ticks.constraint: productive activity limited to daylight hours
ticks.detail: Electrification is the substrate for virtually all that follows.

links.label: Wikipedia: History of electric power transmission
Jill Jonnes — Empires of Light (Edison vs Tesla)

ticks.name: Rabies vaccine (Pasteur / first viral vaccine)
ticks.constraint: viral disease as having no vaccine option
ticks.detail: Attenuated virus can train immunity without causing disease. All modern vaccines follow this logic.

links.label: Wikipedia: Rabies vaccine (Pasteur / first viral vaccine)
Google Scholar: Rabies vaccine (Pasteur / first viral vaccine)

ticks.name: Eiffel Tower / structural steel
ticks.constraint: tall structures requiring massive masonry bases
ticks.detail: The structural vocabulary of the modern city.

links.label: Google Scholar: Eiffel Tower / structural steel

ticks.name: Principles of Psychology (William James)
ticks.constraint: mind as unitary and fully conscious
ticks.detail: Psychology split from philosophy. Foundation for pragmatism, functionalism, and cognitive psychology.

links.label: Google Scholar: Principles of Psychology (William James)

ticks.name: Cinema (Lumière brothers)
ticks.constraint: storytelling requiring imagination to animate
ticks.detail: A century of film, propaganda, and mass entertainment follows.

ticks.name: X-ray (Röntgen)
ticks.constraint: the body as opaque to inspection
ticks.detail: Surgeons could plan operations without opening the patient.

ticks.name: Radio waves (Marconi)
ticks.constraint: long-distance communication requiring physical wire
ticks.detail: Mass broadcasting — and mass persuasion — was born.

ticks.name: Interpretation of Dreams (Freud)
ticks.constraint: behavior as fully explicable by conscious intention
ticks.detail: The unconscious as causally active. Psychotherapy and 'processing' emotions begin here.

ticks.name: Planck's quantum hypothesis
ticks.constraint: energy as continuously variable
ticks.detail: Nature is granular at the smallest scale. Quantum mechanics, semiconductors, lasers, and MRI all begin here.

ticks.name: Blood typing (Landsteiner)
ticks.constraint: blood transfusion as fatally unpredictable
ticks.detail: ABO blood typing made transfusions safe. Trauma surgery and organ transplantation depend on this tick.

ticks.name: Powered flight (Wright brothers)
ticks.constraint: human movement limited to land and sea
ticks.detail: The world went from weeks-by-ship to hours-by-plane in one human lifetime.

ticks.name: Photoelectric effect / photons (Einstein)
ticks.constraint: light as purely wave-like
ticks.detail: Wave-particle duality. Quantum field theory and the conceptual crisis of quantum mechanics begin here.

ticks.name: Special relativity (Einstein)
ticks.constraint: time and space as absolute and universal
ticks.detail: E=mc² means matter is frozen energy. Atomic energy, nuclear weapons, and MRI machines are direct applications.

links.label: Einstein — On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies (1905) — original paper
Walter Isaacson — Einstein: His Life and Universe

ticks.name: Cajal / neuron doctrine
ticks.constraint: nervous system as a continuous network
ticks.detail: The nervous system consists of discrete neurons communicating across synapses. Every psychoactive drug depends on understanding this.

ticks.name: Cubism (Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon)
ticks.constraint: painting as representing a single viewpoint
ticks.detail: The 20th century's visual language is cubism's consequence.

links.label: Google Scholar: Cubism (Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon)

ticks.name: Haber-Bosch nitrogen fixation
ticks.constraint: nitrogen fertilizer requiring biological sources
ticks.detail: Without Haber-Bosch, Earth could support ~3.5B people. We have 8B.

links.label: Ouyang et al. — Training language models to follow instructions (InstructGPT, 2022)

ticks.name: Brain-computer interface (Neuralink / BrainGate)
ticks.constraint: paralysis as permanently severing communication between brain and world
ticks.detail: Paralyzed patients could control computers using only neural signals.

ticks.name: GPT-4 multimodality / frontier model capabilities
ticks.constraint: AI assistance as text-only and limited to known information
ticks.detail: The question shifted from 'can AI do this?' to 'how do we integrate AI that can?'

ticks.name: Reasoning models (o1/o3, chain-of-thought at inference)
ticks.constraint: AI reasoning as limited to patterns in training data
ticks.detail: Spending more compute at inference time — reasoning step by step — dramatically improved performance on hard problems. The model was solving, not just recalling.

ticks.name: Organized warfare (first armies)
ticks.constraint: conflict as individual or small-group raids
ticks.detail: Permanent settlements created something worth defending — and conquering. The first organized armies emerged alongside the first cities. War became a state function, not just a feature of human aggression. Every military institution, alliance, and strategic doctrine begins here.

ticks.name: Fortification walls (Uruk, Jericho)
ticks.constraint: settlement defense requiring abandonment or flight
ticks.detail: Jericho's walls predate farming by some accounts. Uruk's walls, built under Gilgamesh, were 9km long. Permanent fortification meant you could hold ground. The city as a military unit — the origin of siege warfare, garrison strategy, and the relationship between urban density and defensibility.

ticks.name: Composite bow
ticks.constraint: archery range limited by single-material bow
ticks.detail: Layers of horn, sinew, and wood laminated together produced a bow far more powerful than any single material could achieve. The composite bow gave mounted archers range and penetration that changed the battlefield for 4,000 years. Every steppe nomad empire — Scythian, Mongol, Hunnic — was built on this technology.

ticks.name: Chariot warfare
ticks.constraint: cavalry speed advantage requiring a mounted warrior
ticks.detail: The chariot combined mobility, elevation, and a stable platform for archers. Egypt vs the Hittites at Kadesh (1274 BC) was the first recorded large-scale chariot battle. The Bronze Age military balance of power hinged on who could afford and field the most chariots.

ticks.name: The phalanx (Greek hoplite formation)
ticks.constraint: infantry effectiveness depending on individual warrior skill
ticks.detail: Interlocking shields and coordinated spear thrusts turned individual soldiers into a collective machine. The phalanx democratized warfare — a disciplined citizen army could defeat elite warriors. Alexander's Macedonia extended it into the combined-arms syntagma. The first truly systematic infantry tactic.

links.label: Google Scholar: The phalanx (Greek hoplite formation)

ticks.name: The Art of War (Sun Tzu)
ticks.constraint: military strategy as purely improvisational and commander-dependent
ticks.detail: The first systematic treatise on strategy as a discipline. Sun Tzu's principles — deception, information asymmetry, the importance of logistics, adapting to terrain — remain the foundation of military theory and business strategy. The idea that war is won before it's fought.

links.label: Wikipedia: The Art of War (Sun Tzu)
Google Scholar: The Art of War (Sun Tzu)

ticks.name: Combined arms warfare (Alexander/Philip)
ticks.constraint: battlefield effectiveness requiring dominance in a single arm
ticks.detail: Philip II and Alexander the Great coordinated cavalry, heavy infantry, light infantry, and siege engines as a unified system. Each arm created conditions for the others. The Companion cavalry's hammer-and-anvil with the phalanx was essentially undefeated. Combined arms doctrine still governs modern military thinking.

ticks.name: Roman manipular legion
ticks.constraint: phalanx rigidity on broken terrain
ticks.detail: Rome replaced the Greek phalanx with a flexible formation of maniples — smaller units that could operate independently, adapt to terrain, and rotate frontline soldiers. The legion's articulation gave Rome tactical adaptability its enemies couldn't match. The organizational template for every Western army until gunpowder.

ticks.name: Archimedes' war machines (Syracuse)
ticks.constraint: fortification defense as passive
ticks.detail: Archimedes designed catapults, cranes, and grappling devices that held off a Roman fleet for three years. The application of mathematics to warfare — range calculation, mechanical advantage, projectile physics. The first documented military engineering in service of systematic defense.

ticks.name: Roman military logistics (castra, supply lines)
ticks.constraint: army campaign range limited by foraging
ticks.detail: The Roman legion built a fortified camp (castra) every night — a standard layout troops could construct in hours. Combined with organized supply lines and engineering capability, this extended campaign range and sustained army size far beyond what any previous force could maintain. Logistics as the actual determinant of military power.

links.label: Wikipedia: Roman military logistics (castra, supply lines)
Google Scholar: Roman military logistics (castra, supply lines)

ticks.name: Greek fire (Byzantine incendiary weapon)
ticks.constraint: naval fire attack requiring close contact
ticks.detail: The Byzantine Empire's secret incendiary weapon — likely naphtha-based — could burn on water and resisted extinguishing. Used to destroy Arab fleets attacking Constantinople in 672-678 and 717-718 AD. The first area-denial naval weapon. Also the first documented use of chemistry as a military system.

links.label: Google Scholar: Greek fire (Byzantine incendiary weapon)

ticks.name: Gunpowder weaponized (China, then West)
ticks.constraint: projectile weapons limited by muscle-powered range and force
ticks.detail: Chinese chemists discovered gunpowder in the 9th century seeking immortality elixirs. Fire arrows, bombs, and early guns followed within 200 years. When gunpowder reached Europe via the Islamic world in the 13th century, it began dismantling feudal military hierarchy — castle walls and armored knights both became obsolete.

links.label: Google Scholar: Gunpowder weaponized (China, then West)

ticks.name: Crusades / military religious orders
ticks.constraint: long-distance military campaigns requiring national armies
ticks.detail: The Crusades created a new institutional form: the military religious order (Templars, Hospitallers, Teutonic Knights) — standing professional armies funded by donations, exempt from feudal obligations, with a transnational identity. The first multinational military institutions. Also: the logistical and financial systems developed to fund them seeded European banking.

links.label: Google Scholar: Crusades / military religious orders

ticks.name: Longbow at Crécy / missile dominance
ticks.constraint: armored cavalry as the decisive military arm
ticks.detail: English longbowmen at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415) destroyed French cavalry at range. The longbow could penetrate plate armor at 200 yards. The age of the mounted knight — and the feudal military system built around it — began its end. Missile weapons defeating shock weapons reshaped social hierarchy, not just tactics.

links.label: Wikipedia: Longbow at Crécy / missile dominance
Google Scholar: Longbow at Crécy / missile dominance

ticks.name: Fall of Constantinople / cannon vs. walls
ticks.constraint: fortified city walls as defensible against conventional siege
ticks.detail: Mehmed II's massive Ottoman cannons breached Constantinople's 1,000-year-old walls in 53 days. The same cannon technology that ended the Byzantine Empire made every medieval castle in Europe vulnerable. The Hundred Years' War's last phase was simultaneously a demonstration that gunpowder siege artillery had made the feudal fortification obsolete.

links.label: Wikipedia: Fall of Constantinople / cannon vs. walls
Google Scholar: Fall of Constantinople / cannon vs. walls

ticks.name: Pike and shot formation
ticks.constraint: infantry requiring either missile or shock — not both simultaneously
ticks.detail: Swiss pikemen and Spanish arquebusiers learned to operate as combined units: musketeers fired while pikemen protected them from cavalry. The tercio formation dominated European battlefields for 150 years. The first systematic doctrine for integrating firearms into infantry tactics.

links.label: Google Scholar: Pike and shot formation

ticks.name: Battle of Lepanto / broadside naval warfare
ticks.constraint: naval combat as galley ramming and boarding
ticks.detail: Lepanto demonstrated the dominance of gunpowder artillery aboard sailing ships over oar-powered galleys. The sailing warship with broadside cannons became the decisive naval instrument. This shift gave Atlantic-facing European powers — Portugal, Spain, England, Netherlands — inherent strategic advantages over Mediterranean powers.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Lepanto / broadside naval warfare
Google Scholar: Battle of Lepanto / broadside naval warfare

ticks.name: Gustavus Adolphus military reforms
ticks.constraint: army effectiveness requiring numerical superiority
ticks.detail: The Swedish king introduced lighter, more mobile artillery; standardized drill; linear tactics; and combined-arms integration that produced a smaller, faster, more effective army. The Military Revolution of the 17th century — armies became professional, drilled, and state-funded. The conscript national army follows from these reforms.

links.label: Google Scholar: Gustavus Adolphus military reforms

ticks.name: Levée en masse (French Revolutionary Army)
ticks.constraint: army size limited by professional recruitment and pay
ticks.detail: France mobilized 300,000 citizen-soldiers in a single decree. The nation-in-arms concept transformed war's scale. Napoleon's armies were its product. Mass conscription, national service, and the idea that war is fought by entire societies — not just professional militaries — all begin with this moment.

links.label: Wikipedia: Levée en masse (French Revolutionary Army)
Google Scholar: Levée en masse (French Revolutionary Army)

ticks.name: Napoleon's corps system
ticks.constraint: army command requiring the general to directly oversee all units
ticks.detail: Napoleon organized armies into self-sufficient corps — each with infantry, cavalry, and artillery — that could operate independently but concentrate quickly. A corps could fight an entire enemy army long enough for others to arrive. The operational level of war as a distinct layer between strategy and tactics.

ticks.name: Colt revolver / repeating firearms
ticks.constraint: firearm advantage negated by slow reloading
ticks.detail: The revolver's rotating cylinder allowed six shots before reloading. Combined with the later rifle and cartridge ammunition, repeating firearms fundamentally changed the lethality calculus of war. The American Civil War was the first major conflict to demonstrate industrial-era firepower — and its casualties shocked the world.

links.label: Google Scholar: Colt revolver / repeating firearms

ticks.name: Railroad warfare (American Civil War)
ticks.constraint: army strategic mobility limited by marching speed
ticks.detail: The Civil War was the first major conflict where railroads moved armies strategically. The side that controlled railroads controlled the campaign. Sherman's March was fundamentally a railroad destruction campaign. Every subsequent industrial war — WWI, WWII — was primarily a contest of logistics networks, not just battle lines.

links.label: Google Scholar: Railroad warfare (American Civil War)

ticks.name: Ironclad warships (Monitor vs. Virginia)
ticks.constraint: wooden warships as the basis of naval power
ticks.detail: The battle of the USS Monitor and CSS Virginia (1862) made every wooden warship on Earth obsolete overnight. Iron (then steel) hulls, steam propulsion, and rotating gun turrets defined naval warfare for the next century. The naval arms race that followed — especially Britain vs. Germany — shaped the path to WWI.

links.label: Google Scholar: Ironclad warships (Monitor vs. Virginia)

ticks.name: Maxim gun / machine gun
ticks.constraint: automatic fire requiring multiple shooters
ticks.detail: Hiram Maxim's recoil-operated machine gun could fire 600 rounds per minute with a single operator. The colonial implications were immediate: small European forces could hold off thousands of African or Asian warriors. WWI's static trench warfare was the direct product — machine guns made offensive infantry movement suicidal.

links.label: Google Scholar: Maxim gun / machine gun

ticks.name: WWI chemical weapons (chlorine/mustard gas)
ticks.constraint: area denial requiring physical fortification
ticks.detail: Germany's 1915 chlorine attack at Ypres was the first large-scale use of chemical weapons in war. Mustard gas followed. The psychological impact outlasted the tactical: the specter of chemical attack shaped 20th-century warfare and arms control. The Chemical Weapons Convention (1993) is still responding to 1915.

links.label: Google Scholar: WWI chemical weapons (chlorine/mustard gas)

ticks.name: Tank (Battle of the Somme)
ticks.constraint: machine gun dominance over offensive infantry
ticks.detail: British tanks first appeared at the Somme in 1916. Mechanically unreliable and tactically misused, they nevertheless demonstrated the concept: armored, mobile fire support could cross no-man's land. German shock tactics and Allied armor doctrine converged by 1918. WWII's blitzkrieg was the theory fully realized.

links.label: Google Scholar: Tank (Battle of the Somme)

ticks.name: Submarine warfare (unrestricted)
ticks.constraint: naval blockade requiring surface fleet superiority
ticks.detail: Germany's U-boat campaign proved that submarines could conduct strategic economic warfare independently of surface fleet control. Unrestricted submarine warfare nearly starved Britain and brought the US into WWI. The submarine became the capital weapon of naval strategy, culminating in WWII's Battle of the Atlantic.

ticks.name: Air power doctrine emerges (WWI)
ticks.constraint: military reconnaissance requiring ground observation
ticks.detail: WWI produced reconnaissance aircraft, then fighters to shoot them down, then bombers. By 1918, strategic bombing theory was being articulated: attack the enemy's industrial and civilian base directly. The interwar period saw this formalized by Douhet, Mitchell, and the RAF. WWII tested and largely validated strategic air power as an independent military instrument.

links.label: Google Scholar: Air power doctrine emerges (WWI)

ticks.name: Blitzkrieg doctrine (Poland/France)
ticks.constraint: armored advance requiring infantry consolidation before proceeding
ticks.detail: Germany's Panzer divisions bypassed fortified positions, drove deep into enemy rear areas, and collapsed command structures before defenders could react. Blitzkrieg wasn't a new technology — it was a new doctrine using existing tanks and aircraft. Speed as the decisive variable, not firepower. The concept reshaped every subsequent armored doctrine.

ticks.name: Carrier warfare (Coral Sea/Midway)
ticks.constraint: naval battles requiring surface ships to exchange gunfire
ticks.detail: Coral Sea (May 1942) was the first naval battle where the opposing surface fleets never saw each other — fought entirely by carrier aircraft. Midway (June 1942) decided the Pacific war with dive bombers. The aircraft carrier replaced the battleship as the capital ship of naval power. Naval doctrine worldwide realigned around this in months.

ticks.name: D-Day amphibious doctrine
ticks.constraint: seaborne landings on defended beaches as prohibitively costly
ticks.detail: Operation Overlord was the largest amphibious operation in history — 156,000 troops on day one. It required purpose-built landing craft, artificial harbors, specialized armor, and coordinated deception operations. The doctrine developed for D-Day codified joint operations (air, sea, land) as the standard approach for contested landings.

ticks.name: Strategic bombing doctrine validated and questioned
ticks.constraint: industrial society as resilient to air attack
ticks.detail: WWII's strategic bombing campaigns destroyed German and Japanese industrial capacity — but required far more resources and caused far more civilian casualties than pre-war theorists predicted. The post-war assessments created the precision bombing doctrine that guided air power through Vietnam, Gulf War, and into the era of GPS-guided munitions.

links.label: Wikipedia: Strategic bombing doctrine validated and questioned
Google Scholar: Strategic bombing doctrine validated and questioned

ticks.name: Nuclear deterrence theory (MAD)
ticks.constraint: military superiority as a guarantee of strategic dominance
ticks.detail: The Soviet atomic test (1949) and the H-bomb race produced Mutually Assured Destruction — the doctrine that nuclear war is unwinnable, and therefore rational actors won't start one. MAD replaced victory with stability. Every Cold War crisis — Cuba, Berlin — was navigated within this framework. The most consequential strategic concept in history.

ticks.name: Intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM)
ticks.constraint: nuclear weapons delivery requiring aircraft penetrating defended airspace
ticks.detail: The Soviet R-7 (1957) and US Atlas (1958) could deliver nuclear warheads across continents in 30 minutes, flying above the atmosphere where they couldn't be intercepted. ICBMs made every point on Earth a potential target. They also drove the second-strike capability that stabilized MAD — and made missile defense an arms control crisis.

ticks.name: Counterinsurgency doctrine (Malaya/Vietnam)
ticks.constraint: guerrilla warfare as solvable by conventional military superiority
ticks.detail: The British success in Malaya (1948-1960) against Communist insurgents — using 'hearts and minds' population-centric tactics, intelligence, and isolation of insurgents from their base — was codified as counterinsurgency doctrine. Its mixed results in Vietnam and later Iraq and Afghanistan showed its limits when political conditions weren't right.

ticks.name: Precision-guided munitions (Yom Kippur War)
ticks.constraint: air-to-ground accuracy requiring low-altitude attack runs
ticks.detail: Egyptian and Syrian SAM missiles and wire-guided anti-tank weapons in the 1973 war shocked Western military observers. Meanwhile, US laser-guided bombs ('smart bombs') demonstrated accuracy previously impossible. Precision strike changed the cost-benefit calculus of air power — you needed fewer sorties, fewer aircraft, and fewer aircraft losses to achieve the same effect.

links.label: Google Scholar: Precision-guided munitions (Yom Kippur War)

ticks.name: Gulf War / network-centric warfare
ticks.constraint: battlefield awareness requiring physical reconnaissance and slow intelligence cycles
ticks.detail: Operation Desert Storm demonstrated satellite communications, GPS navigation, stealth aircraft, precision guided munitions, and real-time intelligence integration. The 100-hour ground war with minimal coalition casualties validated a new paradigm: information dominance as a force multiplier. Network-centric warfare doctrine followed.

links.label: Google Scholar: Gulf War / network-centric warfare

ticks.name: Drone warfare / remote combat
ticks.constraint: lethal force requiring physical presence of the operator
ticks.detail: The Predator drone's first armed strike (2001, Afghanistan) began the era of remote killing — a pilot in Nevada guiding a strike in Pakistan. Drone warfare separated risk from lethality, enabling persistent surveillance and precision strike at low cost with zero operator risk. It also fundamentally changed the legal and ethical calculus of war.

links.label: Google Scholar: Drone warfare / remote combat

ticks.name: Ukraine war / commercial drones and OSINT
ticks.constraint: military intelligence requiring classified infrastructure
ticks.detail: The Russia-Ukraine war demonstrated that commercial drones ($500 quadcopters) could locate and destroy multi-million-dollar tanks, that social media posts could track army movements, and that satellite imagery services open to the public could document war crimes in real time. The democratization of battlefield intelligence and aerial attack.

links.label: Wikipedia: Ukraine war / commercial drones and OSINT
Google Scholar: Ukraine war / commercial drones and OSINT

ticks.name: Linnaeus / binomial nomenclature
ticks.constraint: natural history as locally named and regionally incomparable
ticks.detail: Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae gave every species a two-part Latin name — genus and species. For the first time, a botanist in Sweden and one in Brazil could refer to the same plant unambiguously. Taxonomy enabled comparison, accumulation of biological knowledge, and eventually the evolutionary framework that explained the patterns.

ticks.name: Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann)
ticks.constraint: the organizational unit of life as unknown
ticks.detail: Matthias Schleiden (plants) and Theodor Schwann (animals) synthesized the cell theory: all living things are composed of cells. This unified biology — plants, animals, fungi — under a single structural principle. Every subsequent advance in biology, from genetics to cancer biology, is built on the cell as the unit of life.

links.label: Google Scholar: Cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann)

ticks.name: Mendel's inheritance rules
ticks.constraint: heredity as a continuous blending of parental traits
ticks.detail: Gregor Mendel's pea plant experiments (1856-1863, published 1866) showed inheritance is particulate — traits come in discrete units that don't blend. Dominant and recessive. Ignored for 35 years, then recognized as the foundation of genetics. The gene as a concept was implicit in Mendel before anyone knew what DNA was.

ticks.name: Natural selection (Darwin/Wallace)
ticks.constraint: biological diversity requiring a designer
ticks.detail: Darwin and Wallace independently proposed that variation + selection + time = adaptation without any directing intelligence. Evolution by natural selection is the central organizing principle of all biology. It explained the distribution of species, the structure of anatomy, the fossil record — and eventually behavior, psychology, and medicine.

ticks.name: DNA discovered (Miescher)
ticks.constraint: cell nuclei as structurally uniform and functionally unknown
ticks.detail: Friedrich Miescher isolated an acidic substance from white blood cell nuclei in 1869 — what he called 'nuclein,' now known as DNA. He didn't know its function. It took 84 years (until 1953) to understand that this molecule carries hereditary information. The gap between discovery and understanding is one of science's longest.

ticks.name: Germ theory extended to immune response (Metchnikoff)
ticks.constraint: immune defense as chemical and passive
ticks.detail: Élie Metchnikoff discovered phagocytosis — white blood cells actively engulfing and destroying bacteria. The immune system was not a wall but an army. Cellular immunology was born. Every vaccine, immunotherapy, and understanding of autoimmune disease builds on Metchnikoff's observation of a starfish larva eating a rose thorn.

links.label: Wikipedia: Germ theory extended to immune response (Metchnikoff)
Google Scholar: Germ theory extended to immune response (Metchnikoff)

ticks.name: Rediscovery of Mendel / birth of genetics
ticks.constraint: hereditary mechanism as continuous and unknowable
ticks.detail: Three botanists (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak) independently rediscovered Mendel's 1866 paper in 1900. The science of genetics was officially born. Within a decade: chromosomes were identified as the physical carriers of Mendel's 'factors,' and the word 'gene' was coined. Genetics and evolution merged into the Modern Synthesis.

links.label: Wikipedia: Rediscovery of Mendel / birth of genetics
Google Scholar: Rediscovery of Mendel / birth of genetics

ticks.name: Chromosomes as carriers of genes (Morgan)
ticks.constraint: genes as abstract units without physical location
ticks.detail: Thomas Hunt Morgan's Drosophila experiments showed that genes are carried on chromosomes and that linked genes are sometimes separated during reproduction (crossing over). The chromosome theory of heredity was established. Gene mapping became possible — you could know not just that a gene existed, but where it lived.

links.label: Wikipedia: Chromosomes as carriers of genes (Morgan)
Google Scholar: Chromosomes as carriers of genes (Morgan)

ticks.name: Mutation via X-rays (Muller)
ticks.constraint: genetic mutation as a random, uncontrollable event
ticks.detail: Hermann Muller showed that X-ray exposure dramatically increased the mutation rate in Drosophila. Mutations were physical events, caused by physical agents. This opened radiation genetics, the study of mutagens, and eventually the understanding that mutations cause cancer. Also: it alarmed the world about nuclear radiation's biological effects.

ticks.name: DNA as the genetic material (Avery et al.)
ticks.constraint: protein as the presumed carrier of genetic information
ticks.detail: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty showed that the 'transforming principle' — the substance that could permanently alter bacteria — was DNA, not protein. Most scientists didn't believe it. It took nine more years and Watson & Crick's structure to convince the field. The click was definitively identifying the molecule of heredity.

links.label: Wikipedia: DNA as the genetic material (Avery et al.)
Google Scholar: DNA as the genetic material (Avery et al.)

ticks.name: Genetic code / protein synthesis (Crick's central dogma)
ticks.constraint: the mechanism connecting DNA to protein as unknown
ticks.detail: Crick's 'central dogma' (1958): DNA → RNA → Protein. Information flows one way. Sequences of DNA codons specify sequences of amino acids. The genetic code — all 64 triplet codons — was cracked by 1966. Every biotechnology, every gene therapy, every understanding of how cells work depends on this one-way information flow.

links.label: Wikipedia: Genetic code / protein synthesis (Crick's central dogma)
Google Scholar: Genetic code / protein synthesis (Crick's central dogma)

ticks.name: Restriction enzymes discovered
ticks.constraint: DNA as cuttable only by imprecise physical or chemical means
ticks.detail: Werner Arber, Hamilton Smith, and Daniel Nathans discovered restriction enzymes — bacterial proteins that cut DNA at specific sequences. Every recombinant DNA technique, every genetic engineering application, every molecular biology laboratory procedure uses restriction enzymes. They are the scissors of molecular biology.

ticks.name: Genetic code fully cracked
ticks.constraint: the translation of DNA sequences into proteins as unknown
ticks.detail: By 1966, all 64 triplet codons had been mapped to specific amino acids or stop signals. The universal genetic code was complete. The same code operates in bacteria, plants, animals, and humans — confirming universal common descent and enabling the reading of any organism's genes for any purpose.

links.label: Google Scholar: Genetic code fully cracked

ticks.name: Reverse transcriptase (Temin/Baltimore)
ticks.constraint: RNA-to-DNA information transfer as impossible (central dogma violation)
ticks.detail: Howard Temin and David Baltimore independently discovered reverse transcriptase — an enzyme that transcribes RNA back into DNA, apparently violating Crick's central dogma. Actually it extended it. Retroviruses (including HIV) use this mechanism. Reverse transcriptase is also the tool that makes cDNA libraries, PCR, and mRNA vaccines possible.

ticks.name: DNA sequencing (Sanger method)
ticks.constraint: reading DNA sequences as prohibitively slow and expensive
ticks.detail: Frederick Sanger's chain-termination sequencing method made reading DNA sequences practical. The entire Human Genome Project used Sanger sequencing. The cost of sequencing declined from billions to hundreds of dollars. Every genomic medicine application, every evolutionary analysis, every forensic DNA test uses sequencing descended from Sanger's method.

ticks.name: PCR (polymerase chain reaction)
ticks.constraint: DNA analysis requiring large quantities of starting material
ticks.detail: Kary Mullis invented PCR while driving on a California highway. It amplifies tiny DNA samples into millions of copies in hours. Every COVID-19 test, every forensic DNA analysis, every ancient DNA study, every genetic diagnosis uses PCR. Mullis called it 'molecular photocopying.' It made biology's most powerful analytical tool available from a drop of blood.

links.label: Mullis — The Unusual Origin of the Polymerase Chain Reaction (Scientific American 1990)

ticks.name: Gene therapy (first clinical trial)
ticks.constraint: genetic disease as untreatable at its molecular root
ticks.detail: The first human gene therapy trial treated a four-year-old girl with SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) in 1990 by inserting a corrected gene into her white blood cells. It worked partially. The field spent 20 years recovering from setbacks (Jesse Gelsinger's death in 1999). Today: approved gene therapies cure sickle cell disease and hemophilia.

links.label: Google Scholar: Gene therapy (first clinical trial)

ticks.name: BRCA1/2 genes identified (breast cancer genetics)
ticks.constraint: cancer predisposition as unpredictable and un-preventable
ticks.detail: Mary-Claire King's discovery that breast cancer runs in families led to the identification of BRCA1 (1994) and BRCA2 (1995). Genetic testing for cancer predisposition became possible. Preventive mastectomy and oophorectomy could eliminate 80%+ lifetime risk. The principle: cancer risk is partly written in the genome and can be read.

links.label: Wikipedia: BRCA1/2 genes identified (breast cancer genetics)
Google Scholar: BRCA1/2 genes identified (breast cancer genetics)

ticks.name: Dolly the sheep / somatic cell nuclear transfer
ticks.constraint: differentiated adult cells as unable to revert to pluripotency
ticks.detail: Dolly proved that an adult cell's nucleus, placed in an enucleated egg, could produce a complete organism. Differentiation was reversible. This opened therapeutic cloning, stem cell biology, and reprogramming research. Within 10 years, Shinya Yamanaka showed you could reprogram adult cells directly into pluripotent stem cells — without cloning.

links.label: Wikipedia: Dolly the sheep / somatic cell nuclear transfer
Google Scholar: Dolly the sheep / somatic cell nuclear transfer

ticks.name: RNA interference / RNAi (Fire and Mello)
ticks.constraint: gene expression as manageable only by removing or editing the gene
ticks.detail: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello discovered that double-stranded RNA could silence specific genes by triggering their degradation. Gene expression could be turned off with exquisite specificity without altering the genome. RNAi became a research tool, then a therapeutic platform. The first RNAi drug (patisiran) was approved in 2018.

links.label: Wikipedia: RNA interference / RNAi (Fire and Mello)
Google Scholar: RNA interference / RNAi (Fire and Mello)

ticks.name: Human genome sequence completed
ticks.constraint: the complete human genetic blueprint as unknown
ticks.detail: The Human Genome Project's completion in April 2003 (50th anniversary of the double helix) produced the reference sequence for all ~3 billion base pairs. The genome became a searchable, annotatable database. Every genetic disease can now be located. Every evolutionary relationship can be quantified. The book of life was opened.

links.label: Google Scholar: Human genome sequence completed

ticks.name: Induced pluripotent stem cells (Yamanaka)
ticks.constraint: pluripotent stem cells requiring embryo destruction to obtain
ticks.detail: Shinya Yamanaka reprogrammed adult mouse skin cells into pluripotent stem cells using just four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc). The ethical controversy around embryonic stem cells was bypassed. Any patient's cells could become any tissue. Personalized medicine, disease modeling, and drug testing in patient-specific cells became possible.

links.label: Google Scholar: Induced pluripotent stem cells (Yamanaka)

ticks.name: CRISPR-Cas9 as genome editing tool (Doudna/Charpentier)
ticks.constraint: precise genome editing as requiring complex zinc finger or TALEN proteins
ticks.detail: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed to cut any DNA sequence with a simple guide RNA. Genome editing went from a specialist's laboratory art to a standard technique available to any biology lab. The cost dropped 99%. Therapeutic gene editing, agricultural modification, and basic research were all transformed.

links.label: Wikipedia: CRISPR-Cas9 as genome editing tool (Doudna/Charpentier)
Google Scholar: CRISPR-Cas9 as genome editing tool (Doudna/Charpentier)

ticks.name: First CRISPR-edited human embryos (He Jiankui)
ticks.constraint: germline editing as a theoretical future concern
ticks.detail: He Jiankui announced the birth of CRISPR-edited twin girls with a CCR5 mutation intended to confer HIV resistance. The tick: heritable human genetic modification had happened. The scientific community's condemnation was universal. The ethical frameworks, regulatory responses, and international governance conversations that followed are still ongoing.

links.label: Wikipedia: First CRISPR-edited human embryos (He Jiankui)
Google Scholar: First CRISPR-edited human embryos (He Jiankui)

ticks.name: Pfizer/Moderna mRNA vaccines (COVID-19)
ticks.constraint: vaccine development as requiring years of biological manufacturing optimization
ticks.detail: The SARS-CoV-2 sequence was published January 10, 2020. The first mRNA vaccine doses were administered December 2020 — 11 months. The mRNA platform doesn't require growing live virus, just synthesizing RNA. Future vaccines against influenza, HIV, cancer neoantigens, and RSV are being developed using the same platform.

ticks.name: AlphaFold / protein structure revolution
ticks.constraint: protein structure prediction as requiring decades of crystallography
ticks.detail: DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted the structures of virtually all known proteins with atomic accuracy. The database of 200 million structures was released free. Drug discovery, enzyme engineering, and understanding of disease mechanisms were transformed. Described by Nobel laureate Venki Ramakrishnan as 'the most significant advance in biology in decades.'

links.label: Google Scholar: AlphaFold / protein structure revolution

ticks.name: Aristotle's De Anima (theory of mind)
ticks.constraint: mind as separable from the body
ticks.detail: Aristotle argued the soul (psyche) is the form of the body — not a separate substance, but the organizing principle of a living being. This materialist, functionalist account of mind anticipated modern cognitive science by 2,300 years. The mind as what the brain does, not a ghost in a machine.

links.label: Wikipedia: Aristotle's De Anima (theory of mind)
Google Scholar: Aristotle's De Anima (theory of mind)

ticks.name: Descartes / mind-body problem formalized
ticks.constraint: mind and body as obviously unified
ticks.detail: Descartes' Meditations drew a sharp distinction between res cogitans (thinking substance) and res extensa (extended material substance). The mind-body problem — how an immaterial mind can causally interact with a material body — has driven philosophy, neuroscience, and AI ever since. Also: cogito ergo sum as the foundation of modern epistemology.

links.label: Google Scholar: Descartes / mind-body problem formalized

ticks.name: Hume / bundle theory of the self
ticks.constraint: the self as a persisting, unified entity
ticks.detail: David Hume searched his experience for a self and found only a 'bundle of perceptions.' There is no persistent, unified self — only a stream of momentary experiences. This preceded Buddhist psychology's similar insight and anticipates modern neuroscience's challenges to the unified self. Personal identity as a useful fiction, not a metaphysical fact.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hume / bundle theory of the self
Google Scholar: Hume / bundle theory of the self

ticks.name: Phineas Gage / first personality neuroscience
ticks.constraint: character as independent of brain physiology
ticks.detail: An iron rod through the frontal lobe changed Gage from a responsible, careful man to an impulsive, profane one. The first clear demonstration that specific brain damage produces specific personality changes. Modern neuropsychology, the localization of emotion and social behavior in the prefrontal cortex, all trace to this railroad accident.

links.label: Wikipedia: Phineas Gage / first personality neuroscience
Google Scholar: Phineas Gage / first personality neuroscience

ticks.name: Wundt's experimental psychology laboratory
ticks.constraint: psychology as philosophical speculation rather than empirical science
ticks.detail: Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig in 1879 — psychology officially became an experimental discipline. He used introspection under controlled conditions to study reaction times, attention, and perception. The institutionalization of psychology as a science separate from philosophy begins here.

links.label: Google Scholar: Wundt's experimental psychology laboratory

ticks.name: James / stream of consciousness
ticks.constraint: consciousness as composed of discrete, separable mental atoms
ticks.detail: William James's Principles of Psychology argued consciousness is not a collection of distinct mental elements but a continuous, flowing stream. This anticipates phenomenology, cognitive science's rejection of strict behaviorism, and modern theories of attention. Also: James introduced the concept of habit as the basis of character formation.

links.label: Google Scholar: James / stream of consciousness

ticks.name: Freud / unconscious as causally active
ticks.constraint: behavior as fully explicable by conscious intention
ticks.detail: The Interpretation of Dreams proposed the unconscious as a system with its own logic (dream work, wish fulfillment, repression, displacement) that causally determines conscious behavior. Right or wrong in specifics, Freud's framework was the first to systematically argue that mental causation operates below the level of awareness.

links.label: Wikipedia: Freud / unconscious as causally active
Google Scholar: Freud / unconscious as causally active

ticks.name: Binet-Simon intelligence test (IQ)
ticks.constraint: cognitive ability as unmeasurable
ticks.detail: Alfred Binet and Théodore Simon developed the first standardized intelligence test to identify children needing extra help in Paris schools. The concept of a measurable 'mental age' and later IQ (Stern, 1912) launched a century of psychometric science, educational testing, and — controversially — eugenics. The tick that made mind quantifiable.

ticks.name: Watson / behaviorism manifesto
ticks.constraint: psychology as requiring study of inner mental states
ticks.detail: John Watson's 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It' argued psychology should study only observable behavior — stimuli and responses — not unobservable mental events. Radical but productive. Conditioning, reinforcement schedules, and learning theory all emerged from behaviorism. It dominated until the cognitive revolution of the 1950s.

ticks.name: Rorschach inkblot test
ticks.constraint: unconscious thought patterns as inaccessible to external observation
ticks.detail: Hermann Rorschach's projective test assumed that how people interpret ambiguous images reveals unconscious mental patterns. Validity remains contested, but the test established projective assessment as a clinical tool and the broader principle that responses to ambiguous stimuli can reveal personality structure.

ticks.name: Piaget / cognitive development stages
ticks.constraint: children as small, incomplete adults cognitively
ticks.detail: Jean Piaget's observation of his own children led to the theory that cognitive development proceeds through qualitatively distinct stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational) — children don't just know less than adults, they think differently. Developmental psychology, educational design, and child-centered pedagogy all follow.

links.label: Google Scholar: Piaget / cognitive development stages

ticks.name: Stroop effect / cognitive interference
ticks.constraint: automatic and controlled processes as separable
ticks.detail: The Stroop task — naming the ink color of color words (e.g., 'RED' written in blue) — demonstrated that automatic reading interferes with controlled color-naming. It showed that mental processes compete for resources and that automaticity creates interference. Cognitive psychology's evidence for dual-process theory begins here.

links.label: Google Scholar: Stroop effect / cognitive interference

ticks.name: Skinner box / operant conditioning
ticks.constraint: behavior change as requiring conscious understanding of the contingency
ticks.detail: B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning chamber showed that behavior is shaped by its consequences — reinforcement increases frequency, punishment decreases it — without the organism needing to understand why. Behavior modification, token economies, video game design, social media like buttons, and slot machines all use Skinnerian principles.

links.label: Google Scholar: Skinner box / operant conditioning

ticks.name: McCulloch-Pitts / first mathematical neuron
ticks.constraint: neural computation as beyond mathematical modeling
ticks.detail: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published 'A Logical Calculus of Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' — a mathematical model of a neuron as a binary threshold device. The first formal description of computation in neural terms. It directly inspired von Neumann's computer architecture and the entire field of artificial neural networks.

links.label: Google Scholar: McCulloch-Pitts / first mathematical neuron

ticks.name: Hebb's rule / synaptic plasticity
ticks.constraint: the brain as a fixed, unchanging structure
ticks.detail: Donald Hebb's rule: 'neurons that fire together, wire together.' Synaptic connections strengthen with correlated activity. The first mechanistic account of learning at the neural level. Long-term potentiation (confirmed experimentally in 1966), memory consolidation, and the entire field of synaptic plasticity all build on Hebb's rule.

links.label: Google Scholar: Hebb's rule / synaptic plasticity

ticks.name: Turing test / machine intelligence
ticks.constraint: intelligence as exclusively biological
ticks.detail: Alan Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' proposed the imitation game as a criterion for machine intelligence: if a machine can converse indistinguishably from a human, it should be considered intelligent. The paper launched AI as a field, sparked 70 years of philosophical debate, and framed the question of machine consciousness that still has no answer.

links.label: Google Scholar: Turing test / machine intelligence

ticks.name: George Miller / working memory limits (7±2)
ticks.constraint: working memory capacity as unlimited or undefined
ticks.detail: Miller's 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' established that working memory holds roughly 7 items. Chunking — organizing information into larger units — can extend this. UI design, instructional design, and cognitive load theory all use Miller's finding. It also launched cognitive psychology's project of mapping the architecture of the mind.

links.label: Wikipedia: George Miller / working memory limits (7±2)
Google Scholar: George Miller / working memory limits (7±2)

ticks.name: Milgram obedience experiments
ticks.constraint: destructive obedience as limited to pathological personalities
ticks.detail: Stanley Milgram showed that ordinary Americans would administer apparently lethal electric shocks to strangers on the instruction of an authority figure — 65% went to the maximum. The tick: context and authority structures, not personal pathology, explain most destructive human behavior. The implications for institutional design and ethics were profound.

ticks.name: Stanford Prison Experiment
ticks.constraint: prison guard brutality as a selection effect (bad people becoming guards)
ticks.detail: Philip Zimbardo's simulated prison produced guard brutality and prisoner submission within days. The tick: ordinary people, placed in roles and systems, enact those roles' worst features without any selection for cruelty. Situationism vs. dispositionism. The experiment shaped organizational psychology, prison reform debates, and ethics review requirements.

ticks.name: Tversky and Kahneman / heuristics and biases
ticks.constraint: human judgment errors as random noise rather than systematic patterns
ticks.detail: The 1972-1974 papers on representativeness, availability, and anchoring showed that human judgment errors are not random but systematic and predictable. The mind uses cognitive shortcuts (heuristics) that produce characteristic biases. Behavioral economics, nudge policy, and the design of choice architecture all follow from this research program.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tversky and Kahneman / heuristics and biases
Google Scholar: Tversky and Kahneman / heuristics and biases

ticks.name: Sociobiology (E.O. Wilson)
ticks.constraint: social behavior as purely cultural and learning-based
ticks.detail: Wilson's Sociobiology argued that social behavior in animals — including humans — is partly shaped by natural selection. The hypothesis that human psychology has an evolutionary architecture — kin selection, reciprocal altruism, status competition — launched evolutionary psychology. Hugely controversial, and still contested, but the framework proved productive.

ticks.name: Split-brain research / two hemispheres (Sperry)
ticks.constraint: the brain as a unified information-processing system
ticks.detail: Roger Sperry's split-brain patients (whose corpus callosum was severed for epilepsy) showed that the two hemispheres can operate independently, with different specializations (language in left, spatial in right). The tick: 'the brain' is not one system but a confederation of systems that normally communicate through the corpus callosum.

links.label: Google Scholar: Split-brain research / two hemispheres (Sperry)

ticks.name: Multiple intelligences theory (Gardner)
ticks.constraint: intelligence as a single, general-purpose faculty (g)
ticks.detail: Howard Gardner's Frames of Mind proposed at least seven distinct intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, spatial, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal. Contested scientifically but enormously influential in education. The tick: 'smart' is not one thing. Educational practice, gifted programs, and assessment design were all affected.

ticks.name: Implicit Association Test (IAT)
ticks.constraint: prejudice as accessible only through self-report
ticks.detail: The IAT measures the speed of associations between concepts, revealing implicit biases that people often don't consciously hold or report. It showed that attitudes exist at multiple levels — explicit and implicit — and that the implicit level often predicts behavior better. Diversity training, legal scholarship on implicit bias, and hiring practice were all affected.

ticks.name: Somatic marker hypothesis (Damasio)
ticks.constraint: emotion as an impediment to rational decision-making
