ticks.detail: Antonio Damasio's patients with ventromedial prefrontal damage had intact logic but terrible real-world decisions — they couldn't feel the emotional significance of options. His somatic marker hypothesis: emotion is not opposed to reason, it is a necessary input. Rationality requires emotional guidance. Every behavioral economics intervention builds on this.

ticks.name: Nudge theory / libertarian paternalism (Thaler/Sunstein)
ticks.constraint: behavior change requiring legislation or incentive redesign
ticks.detail: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein formalized nudge theory: you can change behavior by redesigning the choice architecture — default options, framing, social norms — without restricting choice or changing incentives. Automatic pension enrollment, organ donation opt-out defaults, and cafeteria food placement are all nudges. Governments worldwide adopted nudge units.

links.label: Google Scholar: Nudge theory / libertarian paternalism (Thaler/Sunstein)

ticks.name: Default mode network / mind-wandering neuroscience
ticks.constraint: resting brain as inactive and unimportant
ticks.detail: fMRI studies showed the brain is highly active during 'rest' — a network (default mode network) activates when people are not focused on external tasks. Mind-wandering, self-referential thought, and creativity all involve the DMN. The insight: what the brain does when 'doing nothing' is as important as what it does during tasks.

links.label: Wikipedia: Default mode network / mind-wandering neuroscience
Google Scholar: Default mode network / mind-wandering neuroscience

ticks.name: Large-scale replication crisis formalized
ticks.constraint: published psychology findings as reliable and reproducible
ticks.detail: The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 replication project found that only 36% of 100 psychology studies replicated. The replication crisis prompted widespread adoption of pre-registration, open data, and larger sample sizes. The tick: the methods that produced a century of psychological findings were systematically insufficient for the claims they supported.

links.label: Google Scholar: Large-scale replication crisis formalized

ticks.name: Census and taxation (Ur III)
ticks.constraint: state revenue requiring the ruler to personally assess each subject
ticks.detail: The Ur III dynasty (2112-2004 BC) conducted the ancient world's most sophisticated administrative census — tracking people, cattle, fields, and labor obligations. This administrative state, backed by writing and standardized units, enabled taxation at scale. Every modern state's fiscal apparatus is a descendent of Ur's clay tablets.

links.label: Google Scholar: Census and taxation (Ur III)

ticks.name: Money as abstract exchange medium
ticks.constraint: exchange requiring coincidence of wants between trading parties
ticks.detail: The first coins in Lydia (600 BC) formalized what Mesopotamia had been doing with silver shekels for millennia. Abstract exchange — trading a cow for a claim on future goods — unlocked specialization, markets, and long-distance trade. Money as a social technology solved the double coincidence of wants problem and enabled civilization's complexity.

links.label: Wikipedia: Money as abstract exchange medium
Google Scholar: Money as abstract exchange medium

ticks.name: Olympic Games / pan-Hellenic identity
ticks.constraint: Greek political identity as purely city-state-local
ticks.detail: The Olympic Games created a shared cultural space for competing city-states — a four-year truce, shared religious ritual, common heroes. The first international institution. The idea that rivalrous political units can share a common cultural framework — sports, festivals, diplomacy — is the template for all subsequent international institutions.

links.label: Google Scholar: Olympic Games / pan-Hellenic identity

ticks.name: Solon's reforms / debt cancellation
ticks.constraint: debt slavery as permanent and systemic
ticks.detail: Solon's seisachtheia (shaking off of burdens) cancelled agricultural debts and freed Athenians enslaved for debt. The first documented debt jubilee. Also: he reformed the legal code to be written and public. The principle that debt relationships require periodic resetting — and that law can override private contracts in the public interest — recurs throughout history.

links.label: Google Scholar: Solon's reforms / debt cancellation

ticks.name: Roman citizenship / universal civic identity
ticks.constraint: citizenship as ethnically or tribally bounded
ticks.detail: Rome's gradual extension of citizenship to conquered peoples — culminating in Caracalla's Edict (212 AD) granting citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire — created a universal civic identity independent of ethnicity. The model of civic rather than ethnic nationhood that liberal democracy inherited.

links.label: Wikipedia: Roman citizenship / universal civic identity
Google Scholar: Roman citizenship / universal civic identity

ticks.name: Muhammad's recitation / monotheistic social revolution
ticks.constraint: Arabian tribal social organization as the only available framework
ticks.detail: Islam provided a universal social framework transcending tribe and kinship — all Muslims were brothers. Within a century, a new civilization stretched from Spain to Central Asia with a unified legal system (sharia), shared language (Arabic), and common economic practices. The fastest civilizational expansion in history.

links.label: Wikipedia: Muhammad's recitation / monotheistic social revolution
Google Scholar: Muhammad's recitation / monotheistic social revolution

ticks.name: Fourth Lateran Council / confession annual
ticks.constraint: individual spiritual accounting as occasional and voluntary
ticks.detail: The 1215 Council required annual confession from every Catholic Christian. This created an unprecedented apparatus of individual moral accounting — a mandatory annual examination of one's inner life reported to a priest. Historians argue it created a distinctly Western interiority, privacy concept, and individual conscience that shaped European civilization.

links.label: Wikipedia: Fourth Lateran Council / confession annual
Google Scholar: Fourth Lateran Council / confession annual

ticks.name: Printing press and the Reformation
ticks.constraint: religious authority requiring control of text production
ticks.detail: Martin Luther's 95 Theses (1517) became a European phenomenon within weeks because of the printing press. The Reformation was fundamentally an information revolution — doctrinal debates that had previously stayed within clerical circles were now broadcast to literate laypeople. The state-church synthesis of medieval Europe was the casualty.

links.label: Wikipedia: Printing press and the Reformation
Google Scholar: Printing press and the Reformation

ticks.name: Protestant Reformation (Luther's 95 Theses)
ticks.constraint: Christian religious authority as unified under Rome
ticks.detail: Luther's challenge to indulgences was not new — Hus and Wycliffe had said similar things — but the printing press made it unstoppable. Protestantism fractured European Christianity permanently. Religious wars, the Peace of Westphalia, the concept of religious toleration, secular sovereignty, and eventually the separation of church and state all follow.

ticks.name: Columbian Exchange / demographic catastrophe
ticks.constraint: American Indigenous population as resilient to Old World disease
ticks.detail: Within a century of Columbus, 90% of the Americas' indigenous population died — primarily from epidemic disease (smallpox, measles, typhus). This was the largest demographic catastrophe in human history. It made the colonial project of settlement possible. Understanding it as disease rather than divine providence took centuries.

links.label: Google Scholar: Columbian Exchange / demographic catastrophe

ticks.name: Peace of Westphalia / sovereign state system
ticks.constraint: European political order as hierarchical (pope/emperor at top)
ticks.detail: The Peace of Westphalia ending the Thirty Years' War established the principle of sovereign equality — states are the basic units of international order, each sovereign within its own territory, none subordinate to any external authority. The Westphalian system is still the foundation of international law, the UN Charter, and non-interference doctrine.

links.label: Wikipedia: Peace of Westphalia / sovereign state system
Google Scholar: Peace of Westphalia / sovereign state system

ticks.name: Locke's Two Treatises / natural rights
ticks.constraint: political authority as divinely granted to monarchs
ticks.detail: John Locke argued that legitimate government requires the consent of the governed, that individuals have natural rights (life, liberty, property) that pre-exist government, and that a government that violates these rights can be overthrown. The American Declaration of Independence is almost a paraphrase of Locke. Constitutional liberalism's intellectual foundation.

links.label: Wikipedia: Locke's Two Treatises / natural rights
Google Scholar: Locke's Two Treatises / natural rights

ticks.name: American Declaration of Independence
ticks.constraint: political legitimacy as requiring hereditary or divine authority
ticks.detail: 'All men are created equal' and 'endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights' made equality and natural rights the founding premises of a modern state for the first time. The Declaration was a tick in political philosophy made instantaneous political reality. Every subsequent democratic revolution invokes its language.

links.label: Google Scholar: American Declaration of Independence

ticks.name: French Revolution / popular sovereignty
ticks.constraint: sovereignty as vested in the monarch
ticks.detail: The French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man asserted that sovereignty resides in the nation, not the king. The guillotine removed the king physically; the Declaration removed the principle of monarchy. Nationalism, popular sovereignty, and the modern state all crystallize here. Also: the first modern political terror.

links.label: Google Scholar: French Revolution / popular sovereignty

ticks.name: Abolition of the slave trade (British Empire)
ticks.constraint: economic profitability as sufficient justification for human commodification
ticks.detail: The Slave Trade Act made the transatlantic slave trade illegal for British subjects. William Wilberforce's campaign established the principle — for the first time in history — that a profitable economic institution could be abolished on moral grounds. The abolition movement became the template for all subsequent human rights campaigns.

links.label: Wikipedia: Abolition of the slave trade (British Empire)
Google Scholar: Abolition of the slave trade (British Empire)

ticks.name: Seneca Falls Convention / women's rights declaration
ticks.constraint: political claims-making as exclusively male
ticks.detail: The Declaration of Sentiments at Seneca Falls (1848) asserted that 'all men and women are created equal' — explicitly extending the Declaration of Independence to women. The organized women's rights movement was born. Suffrage, property rights, and eventually full legal equality all trace to this convention in upstate New York.

links.label: Wikipedia: Seneca Falls Convention / women's rights declaration
Google Scholar: Seneca Falls Convention / women's rights declaration

ticks.name: Emancipation Proclamation
ticks.constraint: racial chattel slavery as a permanent constitutional institution in the US
ticks.detail: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation reframed the Civil War from a conflict about union to one about slavery. The 13th Amendment (1865) made it permanent. Four million people were freed. The legal end of slavery in America didn't end racial hierarchy — but it was the constitutional foundation that every subsequent civil rights claim built upon.

ticks.name: International Red Cross / humanitarian law
ticks.constraint: war's treatment of wounded and civilians as entirely at military discretion
ticks.detail: Henri Dunant's founding of the ICRC and the first Geneva Convention created the principle of humanitarian protection in armed conflict. The wounded have rights regardless of which side they fought on. This was radical — war had always been total in its treatment of the vanquished. Humanitarian law is the attempt to keep war within moral limits.

links.label: Wikipedia: International Red Cross / humanitarian law
Google Scholar: International Red Cross / humanitarian law

ticks.name: Berlin Conference / formalization of colonialism
ticks.constraint: African sovereignty from European acknowledgment (perversely)
ticks.detail: The Berlin Conference formalized the 'Scramble for Africa' — European powers divided the continent without African representation. Within 30 years, 90% of Africa was under European colonial rule. The tick: colonialism as a formal international institution with rules (however brutal) rather than ad-hoc conquest. The decolonization movements of the 20th century were responses to this formalization.

links.label: Wikipedia: Berlin Conference / formalization of colonialism
Google Scholar: Berlin Conference / formalization of colonialism

ticks.name: New Zealand first universal suffrage
ticks.constraint: voting as exclusively male
ticks.detail: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant all women the right to vote in national elections. Kate Sheppard's campaign was the model for suffrage movements worldwide. The principle that political citizenship is universal across gender — so obvious it's now unquestioned — was a radical break from 10,000 years of political practice.

links.label: Wikipedia: New Zealand first universal suffrage
Google Scholar: New Zealand first universal suffrage

ticks.name: League of Nations / first world government attempt
ticks.constraint: international relations as purely bilateral between sovereign states
ticks.detail: The League of Nations was the first attempt at a standing international institution with collective security obligations. It failed — largely because the US didn't join and because it had no enforcement mechanism — but it invented the institutional template that the UN improved on. International organizations with permanent bureaucracies, regular meetings, and codified obligations.

links.label: Wikipedia: League of Nations / first world government attempt
Google Scholar: League of Nations / first world government attempt

ticks.name: Nuremberg trials / individual responsibility in international law
ticks.constraint: state officials as immune from personal criminal liability for wartime actions
ticks.detail: The Nuremberg Trials established that individuals can be criminally responsible for crimes against humanity, war crimes, and genocide — even when acting under state orders. 'Following orders' was not a defense. The International Criminal Court, the Responsibility to Protect doctrine, and the entire architecture of international criminal justice builds on Nuremberg.

links.label: Wikipedia: Nuremberg trials / individual responsibility in international law
Google Scholar: Nuremberg trials / individual responsibility in international law

ticks.name: Israeli state / partition and displacement
ticks.constraint: Jewish statelessness as permanent after 2,000 years of diaspora
ticks.detail: The 1948 establishment of Israel was simultaneously a tick for Jewish self-determination and the origin of the Palestinian refugee crisis. Both realities are part of the tick. The creation of a Jewish state resolved the 'Jewish question' posed by European antisemitism in one way while creating a new conflict that has structured Middle Eastern geopolitics ever since.

links.label: Wikipedia: Israeli state / partition and displacement
Google Scholar: Israeli state / partition and displacement

ticks.name: Apartheid institutionalized (South Africa)
ticks.constraint: racial segregation as informal and deniable
ticks.detail: South Africa's National Party institutionalized apartheid in 1948 — a total racial separation system with pass laws, separate homelands, and legal apartheid across every dimension of life. Its formalization made it an international cause that eventually produced comprehensive sanctions and its own end (1994). Nelson Mandela's release and the first democratic election were the counter-tick.

ticks.name: Brown v. Board / legal end of American apartheid
ticks.constraint: racial separation in public institutions as constitutionally permitted
ticks.detail: 'Separate but equal' was inherently unequal. The Supreme Court's unanimous ruling overturned Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and made racial segregation in public schools — and by extension, all public institutions — unconstitutional. The civil rights movement's subsequent legislation (Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965) built directly on Brown.

links.label: Wikipedia: Brown v. Board / legal end of American apartheid
Google Scholar: Brown v. Board / legal end of American apartheid

ticks.name: Cuban Missile Crisis / nuclear diplomacy
ticks.constraint: great power confrontation as inevitably escalatory
ticks.detail: Thirteen days in October 1962 brought the world closer to nuclear war than at any other point. Kennedy and Khrushchev's back-channel diplomacy, the ExComm process, and the eventual solution (US removes missiles from Turkey secretly; Soviets remove missiles from Cuba) established the template for nuclear crisis management. The red phone between Washington and Moscow followed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Cuban Missile Crisis / nuclear diplomacy
Google Scholar: Cuban Missile Crisis / nuclear diplomacy

ticks.name: Moon landing as shared global television event
ticks.constraint: historical events as experienced locally and asynchronously
ticks.detail: 600 million people — roughly 1 in 5 humans alive — watched Neil Armstrong's moonwalk live. It was the first truly global simultaneous shared experience. Television's capacity to create a unified global audience — and eventually a global information environment — was demonstrated. Every subsequent 'television moment' (Berlin Wall, 9/11, COVID) followed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Moon landing as shared global television event
Google Scholar: Moon landing as shared global television event

ticks.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall / end of Cold War
ticks.constraint: the globe as divided between two irreconcilable political-economic systems
ticks.detail: The Wall's fall on November 9, 1989 was both literal and symbolic. Within two years, the Soviet Union had dissolved. The bipolar world order that had governed international relations since 1945 ended. Francis Fukuyama's 'End of History' thesis captured the moment's mood — liberal democracy had won. What replaced the Cold War has been debated ever since.

links.label: Wikipedia: Fall of the Berlin Wall / end of Cold War
Google Scholar: Fall of the Berlin Wall / end of Cold War

ticks.name: Rwandan genocide / failure of international response
ticks.constraint: 'Never Again' as a reliable international commitment
ticks.detail: 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were killed in 100 days while the world watched. The UN peacekeeping force was ordered not to intervene. The genocide exposed the gap between humanitarian rhetoric and political will. It drove the development of the Responsibility to Protect doctrine and the International Criminal Tribunal — but also demonstrated how easily 'Never Again' fails.

links.label: Wikipedia: Rwandan genocide / failure of international response
Google Scholar: Rwandan genocide / failure of international response

ticks.name: 9/11 attacks / global war on terror
ticks.constraint: national security as primarily state-on-state concern
ticks.detail: Non-state actors using box cutters and hijacked aircraft killed 3,000 people and changed global geopolitics. The War on Terror, the Patriot Act, TSA security theater, extraordinary rendition, and the Iraq War all flowed from one morning. The tick: transnational terrorism could reshape the foreign policy of the world's only superpower.

links.label: Wikipedia: 9/11 attacks / global war on terror
Google Scholar: 9/11 attacks / global war on terror

ticks.name: Arab Spring / social media and political revolution
ticks.constraint: authoritarian governments' monopoly on political communication
ticks.detail: Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation triggered protests coordinated via Facebook and Twitter that toppled governments in Tunisia, Egypt, and Libya and shook Syria, Bahrain, and Yemen. Social media as a tool of political organization had been theoretical — the Arab Spring made it demonstrably real. Also real: its limits, as most outcomes were disappointing.

links.label: Wikipedia: Arab Spring / social media and political revolution
Google Scholar: Arab Spring / social media and political revolution

ticks.name: Brexit referendum / populist disruption of expert consensus
ticks.constraint: liberal technocratic consensus as politically unchallengeable
ticks.detail: Britain voted 52-48% to leave the European Union against the recommendation of essentially every major economic and political institution. The tick: populist mobilization against expert consensus, enabled by social media and information fragmentation, could produce irreversible systemic outcomes. Brexit presaged Trump's 2016 election and the broader populist wave.

links.label: Wikipedia: Brexit referendum / populist disruption of expert consensus
Google Scholar: Brexit referendum / populist disruption of expert consensus

ticks.name: Animism / first religion
ticks.constraint: the world as morally neutral and spiritually empty
ticks.detail: The earliest evidence of spiritual belief — the Shanidar Cave Neanderthal burial with flowers, the Aurignacian lion-man figurine — suggests Homo sapiens endowed the natural world with spirits, intentions, and moral significance. Animism was the first framework for understanding why things happen. Every subsequent religion builds on the animist foundation.

ticks.name: Gilgamesh Epic / first literary theology
ticks.constraint: divine relationships as purely ritual and transactional
ticks.detail: The Epic of Gilgamesh (c.2100 BC) is humanity's oldest surviving major literary work and the first to grapple with mortality, friendship, divine will, and the meaning of civilization. It contains a flood narrative nearly identical to Noah's. The first evidence of narrative theology — using story to explore the relationship between humans and the divine.

links.label: Wikipedia: Gilgamesh Epic / first literary theology
Google Scholar: Gilgamesh Epic / first literary theology

ticks.name: Zoroastrianism / cosmic dualism
ticks.constraint: divine action as arbitrary and polytheistic
ticks.detail: Zarathustra's religious reform introduced cosmic moral dualism — Ahura Mazda (truth/good) vs. Angra Mainyu (lie/evil) — with individual souls choosing between them and judgment after death. Zoroastrian concepts of heaven, hell, judgment day, Satan, and apocalypse directly shaped Judaism (during the Babylonian exile), then Christianity and Islam.

ticks.name: Jainism / radical non-violence (ahimsa)
ticks.constraint: religious merit as requiring ritual sacrifice or priestly mediation
ticks.detail: Mahavira's Jainism centered on ahimsa (non-violence toward all living beings), non-attachment, and individual spiritual liberation through ethical conduct — no priest, no god, no sacrifice. The principle that ethical conduct toward all sentient beings is the primary religious obligation. Jain ethics influenced Gandhi's non-violence, which influenced the global civil rights tradition.

ticks.name: Buddha's parinirvana / institutionalized Buddhism
ticks.constraint: spiritual teaching as dying with its teacher
ticks.detail: The Buddha's death prompted his followers to memorize and transmit his teachings, eventually codifying them in the Pali Canon. The sangha (monastic community) became the institutional vehicle for Buddhism's spread. Within 300 years, Buddhism had reached Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and China — the fastest spread of any religion before Islam, and without political force.

links.label: Google Scholar: Buddha's parinirvana / institutionalized Buddhism

ticks.name: Christianity / universal salvation message
ticks.constraint: divine covenant as ethnically or tribally bounded
ticks.detail: Jesus's teaching that salvation was available to all people — Jew and Gentile, slave and free, male and female — was a radical universalism. Paul's letters elaborated this into a theology that could spread across the Roman Empire. Christianity's universalism — the idea that a single religious truth applies to all humanity — changed the world's civilizational architecture.

links.label: Google Scholar: Christianity / universal salvation message

ticks.name: Muhammad's first revelation / Quranic revelation
ticks.constraint: divine revelation as confined to a single people or tradition
ticks.detail: The Quran's claim to be the final, universal revelation — correcting and completing previous scriptures — produced a religion explicitly designed for all humanity. Islam's rapid spread was partly military, but also theological: a simple, memorizable creed (shahada), direct relationship with God (no clergy required), and a practical legal framework applicable anywhere.

links.label: Wikipedia: Muhammad's first revelation / Quranic revelation
Google Scholar: Muhammad's first revelation / Quranic revelation

ticks.name: Great Schism / Eastern and Western Christianity
ticks.constraint: Christian institutional unity as permanent
ticks.detail: The mutual excommunication of Rome and Constantinople split Christianity into Catholic and Orthodox branches. The Filioque controversy (whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from Father and Son) was the theological pretext; the real issue was papal authority. Two distinct civilizational streams — Western and Eastern Europe — diverged at this moment.

links.label: Wikipedia: Great Schism / Eastern and Western Christianity
Google Scholar: Great Schism / Eastern and Western Christianity

ticks.name: Magna Carta / rule of law over divine right
ticks.constraint: monarch's claim to rule by divine right as unchallenged
ticks.detail: Though Magna Carta is primarily a legal document, its assertion that even the king is subject to law challenged the theological foundation of medieval monarchy: the idea that kings ruled by divine appointment. The long-term implication was the secularization of political authority — legitimacy from law, not God.

links.label: Wikipedia: Magna Carta / rule of law over divine right
Google Scholar: Magna Carta / rule of law over divine right

ticks.name: Luther's 95 Theses / Reformation
ticks.constraint: the Catholic Church's monopoly on Christian religious authority
ticks.detail: Luther's challenge to indulgences quickly became a challenge to papal authority itself — his 'sola scriptura' (scripture alone) principle bypassed the Church's interpretive monopoly entirely. The Reformation didn't just split Christianity; it created the concept of conscience against institution, individual against church, text against tradition.

ticks.name: Copernicus / religion confronts cosmology
ticks.constraint: Earth's central position as theological necessity
ticks.detail: De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium moved Earth from the center of creation. This wasn't primarily a religious crisis immediately — Copernicus was a canon of the Church — but Galileo's confirmation using the telescope forced the confrontation. The Galileo affair defined the relationship between religious authority and empirical science for centuries.

links.label: Google Scholar: Copernicus / religion confronts cosmology

ticks.name: Galileo's trial / science vs. institutional religion
ticks.constraint: natural philosophy as subordinate to theological authority
ticks.detail: The Inquisition forced Galileo to recant heliocentrism. The trial defined the conflict between empirical inquiry and religious authority that would shape European intellectual history. Voltaire, the philosophes, and the Enlightenment assault on religious authority all referenced Galileo. The tick: institutional religion had staked its authority on a factual claim that was demonstrably wrong.

links.label: Wikipedia: Galileo's trial / science vs. institutional religion
Google Scholar: Galileo's trial / science vs. institutional religion

ticks.name: Hobbes' Leviathan / secular political theory
ticks.constraint: political philosophy as requiring theological foundation
ticks.detail: Hobbes derived political authority from a purely secular basis: the social contract to escape the 'state of nature' (war of all against all). The sovereign's legitimacy came from its power to provide security, not from divine appointment. Secular political philosophy — politics analyzable without reference to God's will — begins here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hobbes' Leviathan / secular political theory
Google Scholar: Hobbes' Leviathan / secular political theory

ticks.name: Spinoza's Tractatus / biblical criticism
ticks.constraint: sacred texts as literally true and divinely authored
ticks.detail: Spinoza argued that the Bible was a human document, authored by humans in particular historical contexts, and should be interpreted historically and critically. Higher biblical criticism — treating scripture as literature to be analyzed — begins here. Every subsequent liberal theology, every secular biblical scholarship tradition, follows Spinoza's method.

links.label: Google Scholar: Spinoza's Tractatus / biblical criticism

ticks.name: Newton's natural theology / God as first cause
ticks.constraint: science and religion as necessarily opposed
ticks.detail: Newton believed his physics revealed God's rational design of the universe. Natural theology — the attempt to find God through reason and observation — became the dominant mode of 18th-century religious thought. It persisted until Darwin made the argument from design untenable. The dialogue between natural science and religious thought that Newton initiated continues.

links.label: Wikipedia: Newton's natural theology / God as first cause
Google Scholar: Newton's natural theology / God as first cause

ticks.name: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason
ticks.constraint: metaphysics as capable of yielding knowledge of God, freedom, and immortality
ticks.detail: Kant argued that pure reason, unaided by experience, cannot establish knowledge of God, the soul, or free will — these lie beyond the bounds of possible experience. But he rescued them as postulates of practical reason (ethics). The critique ended rationalist metaphysics as Descartes and Leibniz had practiced it and defined the limits of human knowledge.

links.label: Wikipedia: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason
Google Scholar: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason

ticks.name: French Revolution / dechristianization
ticks.constraint: Christianity as Europe's default civic religion
ticks.detail: The Revolution's radical phase attempted to replace Christianity with the Cult of Reason and then the Cult of the Supreme Being — rational, deistic alternatives to Catholicism. It failed, but it established secularism — the separation of religious and civic life — as a political possibility. France's laïcité principle traces directly to 1789.

ticks.name: Baha'i faith / religious universalism
ticks.constraint: each major religion's claim to exclusive final truth
ticks.detail: The Bab's 1844 declaration began what became the Baha'i faith — the belief that all major religions are successive revelations of one God, that humanity is one, and that their unification is both possible and necessary. A tick in religious evolution: a new religion explicitly premised on the unity of all previous ones.

links.label: Google Scholar: Baha'i faith / religious universalism

ticks.name: Darwin / evolution and the argument from design
ticks.constraint: biological complexity as requiring an intelligent designer
ticks.detail: Natural selection provided a mechanism for producing complexity without design. The argument from design — Paley's watchmaker — was the most powerful argument for God's existence in the 18th and 19th centuries. Darwin didn't disprove God, but he removed the need for God as an explanation for biological complexity. Theology has been negotiating this ever since.

links.label: Wikipedia: Darwin / evolution and the argument from design
Google Scholar: Darwin / evolution and the argument from design

ticks.name: Nietzsche / death of God
ticks.constraint: Western culture's ability to ground meaning and morality in Christianity
ticks.detail: 'God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.' Nietzsche's madman announced not atheism but a civilizational crisis: Western culture had built its moral order on Christianity, and now that the intellectual foundations of Christianity had collapsed, what would replace it? His diagnosis: nihilism, and his prescription: the revaluation of all values. Still the central challenge of secular ethics.

links.label: Google Scholar: Nietzsche / death of God

ticks.name: Weber's Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
ticks.constraint: capitalism as explicable purely by material conditions
ticks.detail: Max Weber argued that Calvinist Protestantism — particularly the doctrine of predestination and the resulting compulsion to demonstrate one's salvation through worldly success — created the psychological conditions for modern capitalism. Ideas, not just economic forces, shape economic systems. The sociology of religion and economic sociology were both transformed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Weber's Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
Google Scholar: Weber's Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism

ticks.name: Wittgenstein's Tractatus / limits of language
ticks.constraint: philosophy as capable of answering all meaningful questions through logic
ticks.detail: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' Wittgenstein argued that most traditional philosophical problems arise from misuse of language — trying to say things that can only be shown. The Tractatus defined the limits of what language can express. It launched logical positivism and the analytic tradition, then Wittgenstein repudiated it in the Investigations.

links.label: Wikipedia: Wittgenstein's Tractatus / limits of language
Google Scholar: Wittgenstein's Tractatus / limits of language

ticks.name: Heidegger's Being and Time
ticks.constraint: philosophy as primarily about knowledge and representation
ticks.detail: Heidegger argued that the fundamental question is not 'what can we know?' but 'what is Being?' — and that Dasein (human existence) is characterized by its being-in-the-world, temporality, and being-toward-death. Existentialism, phenomenology, hermeneutics, and poststructuralism all draw from Heidegger. Also: his Nazi involvement remains philosophy's central ethical scandal.

links.label: Google Scholar: Heidegger's Being and Time

ticks.name: Sartre's Being and Nothingness / radical freedom
ticks.constraint: human nature as fixed and essence-giving
ticks.detail: 'Existence precedes essence' — humans have no fixed nature; we are what we make ourselves through free choices. Radical freedom, radical responsibility, and the anguish of having to choose without guaranteed foundations. Existentialism's popular explosion in postwar France captured a generation's response to the war's moral catastrophe.

links.label: Wikipedia: Sartre's Being and Nothingness / radical freedom
Google Scholar: Sartre's Being and Nothingness / radical freedom

ticks.name: Vatican II / Catholic Church's modernization
ticks.constraint: the Catholic Church's stance toward modernity as primarily hostile
ticks.detail: Vatican II's aggiornamento ('bringing up to date') reversed centuries of Catholic suspicion of liberalism, science, and religious pluralism. Mass was said in vernacular languages; the Church acknowledged truth in other religions; ecumenism replaced condemnation. The largest institutional reform in Christian history. Its interpretation continues to divide the Church.

links.label: Wikipedia: Vatican II / Catholic Church's modernization
Google Scholar: Vatican II / Catholic Church's modernization

ticks.name: Rawls' Theory of Justice
ticks.constraint: political philosophy as either utilitarian or natural rights based
ticks.detail: John Rawls revived social contract theory with the 'veil of ignorance' — principles of justice are those we would choose if we didn't know our place in society. The difference principle (inequalities are just only if they benefit the worst-off) provided a rigorous liberal egalitarian framework. Every subsequent political philosophy debate takes Rawls as its starting point.

links.label: Google Scholar: Rawls' Theory of Justice

ticks.name: Singer's Animal Liberation / effective altruism roots
ticks.constraint: moral consideration as limited to humans
ticks.detail: Peter Singer's utilitarian argument that suffering capacity, not species membership, determines moral status launched the modern animal rights movement. Also: his later work on effective altruism (give to maximize impact, not to feel good) created a movement that has redirected billions in charitable giving. Both strands trace to the same utilitarian premise.

links.label: Wikipedia: Singer's Animal Liberation / effective altruism roots
Google Scholar: Singer's Animal Liberation / effective altruism roots

ticks.name: Cattle domestication (aurochs to Bos taurus)
ticks.constraint: cattle as purely hunted game requiring enormous cooperative effort
ticks.detail: The domestication of aurochs into cattle — independently in the Near East, Africa, and South Asia — provided milk, draft power, and meat year-round. The plow pulled by oxen expanded agricultural area dramatically. Cattle created the caloric surplus that built complex societies. Also: cattle represent wealth in most early civilizations, creating the first pastoralist economies.

links.label: Wikipedia: Cattle domestication (aurochs to Bos taurus)
Google Scholar: Cattle domestication (aurochs to Bos taurus)

ticks.name: Rice domestication (Yangtze Valley)
ticks.constraint: East Asian food security as dependent on millet and tubers
ticks.detail: Rice domestication in China's Yangtze Valley began around 7000 BC and spread across Asia over millennia. Wet rice agriculture fed densities of population that no other grain could sustain — enabling East Asian civilizational complexity. Today rice feeds half the world's people. The domestication of rice was as consequential for Asia as wheat was for the Near East.

ticks.name: Plow agriculture
ticks.constraint: soil turning as requiring intensive human or hand labor
ticks.detail: The ard (scratch plow) and later the moldboard plow allowed draft animals to break and turn soil far more efficiently than human hands. Arable land area expanded. Larger fields could be cultivated by fewer people, releasing labor for specialization. The agricultural surplus that built cities depended on the plow.

ticks.name: Three-field crop rotation (Medieval Europe)
ticks.constraint: annual soil exhaustion requiring fallow of 50% of arable land
ticks.detail: Medieval European farmers developed the three-field system: one field planted in autumn, one in spring, one left fallow — rotating annually. Fallow dropped from 50% to 33% of land. The additional field produced legumes (beans, peas) that fixed nitrogen. Agricultural output increased 30-50%. Population grew. European civilization's medieval expansion was built on this rotation.

links.label: Google Scholar: Three-field crop rotation (Medieval Europe)

ticks.name: Potato introduction to Europe
ticks.constraint: European caloric yield per acre as limited by grain crops
ticks.detail: The potato, domesticated in the Andes 8,000 years ago, arrived in Europe in the 1590s. It produces more calories per acre than any grain, grows in poor soil, and resists many diseases. By 1800 it was feeding Ireland, Germany, and much of Northern Europe. The European population explosion of 1750-1850 was substantially a potato story. The 1845 Irish famine shows its vulnerability.

links.label: Google Scholar: Potato introduction to Europe

ticks.name: Maize / corn global spread
ticks.constraint: African, Asian, and Southern European grain options as the only staple choices
ticks.detail: Maize (corn), domesticated in Mexico ~9,000 years ago, spread globally after Columbus. In Africa, it fed populations that sorghum and millet couldn't sustain as densely. In China, it allowed cultivation of hill country previously unusable. The caloric floor of much of sub-Saharan Africa and Southern China was raised by maize. Also: US industrial corn is now a global food system commodity.

links.label: Google Scholar: Maize / corn global spread

ticks.name: Chemical fertilizer (Liebig's mineral theory)
ticks.constraint: soil fertility as a mystical property requiring organic matter
ticks.detail: Justus von Liebig identified nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium as the specific mineral nutrients plants require. Plants don't need 'humus' — they need specific chemicals. This led directly to the synthetic fertilizer industry and the Haber-Bosch process. Liebig's mistake (he undervalued organic matter) created a century of soil degradation, but his insight fed billions.

links.label: Google Scholar: Chemical fertilizer (Liebig's mineral theory)

ticks.name: Refrigeration / cold chain
ticks.constraint: food distribution range limited by spoilage time
ticks.detail: Mechanical refrigeration (Linde's ice machine, 1876) and refrigerated rail cars transformed food geography. Beef from Chicago could reach New York; Argentine beef could reach London. The cold chain decoupled food production from consumption geography. Urban populations could be fed from distant farms. Industrial food systems — and industrial-scale livestock — became possible.

ticks.name: Pasteurization of milk
ticks.constraint: milk as a vector for tuberculosis, typhoid, and scarlet fever
ticks.detail: Louis Pasteur's heating method, applied to milk in the 1880s and mandated in New York City in 1908, eliminated milk-borne disease. Infant mortality dropped dramatically. Pasteurization is estimated to have saved more lives than almost any other public health intervention. It also enabled commercial dairy — milk that could be shipped, stored, and sold safely.

ticks.name: Haber-Bosch process / synthetic nitrogen
ticks.constraint: global nitrogen fertilizer supply limited by guano and Chilean nitrate mines
ticks.detail: Fritz Haber's synthesis of ammonia and Carl Bosch's industrial scaling (completed 1913) created limitless synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. Today, roughly half the nitrogen in human bodies came through the Haber-Bosch process — it's estimated to support 3-4 billion additional people beyond what biological nitrogen fixation alone could feed. The most consequential chemistry in history.

links.label: Google Scholar: Haber-Bosch process / synthetic nitrogen

ticks.name: Green Revolution (Borlaug begins wheat breeding)
ticks.constraint: crop yield as limited by traditional variety genetics
ticks.detail: Norman Borlaug's high-yield, disease-resistant wheat varieties, combined with irrigation and fertilizer, transformed food production in Mexico, India, Pakistan, and later Africa. India went from food aid recipient to food exporter within a decade. The Green Revolution is estimated to have saved a billion lives. Critics note its dependence on chemical inputs and water, and its displacement of agricultural biodiversity.

links.label: Wikipedia: Green Revolution (Borlaug begins wheat breeding)
Google Scholar: Green Revolution (Borlaug begins wheat breeding)

ticks.name: DNA structure enables crop genetic improvement
ticks.constraint: plant breeding as limited to phenotypic selection without mechanistic understanding
ticks.detail: Understanding DNA's structure eventually enabled molecular marker-assisted breeding — selecting for specific genetic variants associated with yield, disease resistance, and drought tolerance. The gap between Watson & Crick (1953) and its agricultural application was 30 years. Today every major crop variety is bred with molecular tools.

links.label: Wikipedia: DNA structure enables crop genetic improvement
Google Scholar: DNA structure enables crop genetic improvement

ticks.name: Recombinant DNA enables genetically modified crops
ticks.constraint: plant genetic improvement as limited to crossing related species
ticks.detail: Boyer and Cohen's recombinant DNA techniques (1973) eventually enabled the insertion of genes from any organism into crop plants. Bt cotton (1996), herbicide-resistant soybeans, and golden rice (provitamin A) became possible. The regulatory, environmental, and social controversy over GMOs is itself a tick — it shaped agricultural biotechnology's development globally.

links.label: Wikipedia: Recombinant DNA enables genetically modified crops
Google Scholar: Recombinant DNA enables genetically modified crops

ticks.name: Flavr Savr tomato / first GM food approved
ticks.constraint: crop traits as bounded by sexual compatibility between species
ticks.detail: The Flavr Savr tomato, engineered with a gene silencing the softening enzyme, was the first GM food approved for human consumption (1994). It was a commercial failure but established the regulatory and cultural precedents for all subsequent GM food approvals. The 'frankenfoods' debate it triggered still shapes agricultural policy worldwide.

links.label: Wikipedia: Flavr Savr tomato / first GM food approved
Google Scholar: Flavr Savr tomato / first GM food approved

ticks.name: Vertical farming / LED-lit indoor agriculture
ticks.constraint: agriculture as dependent on weather, soil, and geography
ticks.detail: LED technology made artificial lighting economically feasible for crop production. Vertical farms grow leafy greens in controlled indoor environments, using 90% less water, no pesticides, and with 365-day production regardless of climate. While still niche, vertical farming decoupled food production from land and weather for the first time in 10,000 years of agriculture.

links.label: Wikipedia: Vertical farming / LED-lit indoor agriculture
Google Scholar: Vertical farming / LED-lit indoor agriculture

ticks.name: Lab-grown meat (first cultured beef burger)
ticks.constraint: meat production as requiring the slaughter of animals
ticks.detail: Mark Post's team grew the first cultured beef burger from bovine stem cells at Maastricht University in 2013. It cost $300,000. By 2023, cultured chicken was approved for sale in the US. If costs continue to fall, lab-grown meat could eliminate the need for industrial livestock farming — currently responsible for ~15% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

links.label: Wikipedia: Lab-grown meat (first cultured beef burger)
Google Scholar: Lab-grown meat (first cultured beef burger)

ticks.name: AI-optimized precision agriculture
ticks.constraint: fertilizer and pesticide application as uniform across entire fields
ticks.detail: Satellite imagery, soil sensors, drone scouting, and AI analysis now enable application of inputs exactly where needed at the right time. John Deere's See & Spray system applies herbicide to individual weeds rather than entire fields, reducing chemical use by 90%. Precision agriculture makes large-scale farming far more efficient while reducing environmental impact.

ticks.name: Division of labor (Adam Smith's pin factory)
ticks.constraint: manufacturing efficiency as limited by each worker doing the whole task
ticks.detail: Smith's famous pin factory example showed that dividing production into specialized steps — one worker draws wire, another straightens it, another cuts it — raised productivity by a factor of 240. Specialization and the division of labor are the fundamental mechanisms of industrial productivity. Every factory, every supply chain, every gig economy platform implements this insight.

links.label: Wikipedia: Division of labor (Adam Smith's pin factory)
Google Scholar: Division of labor (Adam Smith's pin factory)

ticks.name: Ricardo's comparative advantage
ticks.constraint: international trade as beneficial only to the country with absolute cost advantage
ticks.detail: David Ricardo showed that even if one country can produce everything more cheaply, both countries benefit from specializing in what they're relatively better at and trading. Comparative advantage is the theoretical foundation for free trade, globalization, and WTO rules. It's also the most counterintuitive idea in economics — most people still don't believe it.

ticks.name: Marginal revolution (Jevons/Menger/Walras)
ticks.constraint: value as determined by labor input (classical economics)
ticks.detail: Simultaneously in Britain, Austria, and France in 1871, economists independently proposed that value is determined by marginal utility — the value of the last unit consumed, not the average labor embedded. The diamond-water paradox was solved. Microeconomics as we know it — supply and demand, price theory, optimization — begins here.

ticks.name: Keynes' General Theory / macroeconomics born
ticks.constraint: economics as solely microeconomic, with macro 'the sum of micro'
ticks.detail: Keynes created macroeconomics as a distinct field — the study of aggregate demand, national income, unemployment, and the business cycle. His insight: the economy can get stuck in a bad equilibrium (high unemployment, low output) that market forces alone won't fix. Government fiscal policy is the cure. Macroeconomics, the IMF, and every government's economic policy team are Keynes' legacy.

links.label: Wikipedia: Keynes' General Theory / macroeconomics born
Google Scholar: Keynes' General Theory / macroeconomics born

ticks.name: Hayek's Road to Serfdom / price mechanism
ticks.constraint: central planning as a viable alternative to markets for resource allocation
ticks.detail: Hayek argued that no central authority can aggregate the dispersed, local knowledge needed for efficient resource allocation — prices do this automatically. Central planning inevitably leads to political authoritarianism. The neoliberal movement (Thatcher, Reagan) drew on Hayek. His debate with Keynes defined 20th-century economic policy.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hayek's Road to Serfdom / price mechanism
Google Scholar: Hayek's Road to Serfdom / price mechanism

ticks.name: Arrow-Debreu model / general equilibrium
ticks.constraint: competitive markets' efficiency as an empirical claim rather than proved theorem
ticks.detail: Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu rigorously proved the conditions under which competitive markets reach an efficient equilibrium. The proof was also a diagnosis of when markets fail: public goods, externalities, information asymmetries. Modern market failure theory, and the justification for government intervention in markets, builds on Arrow-Debreu.

links.label: Google Scholar: Arrow-Debreu model / general equilibrium

ticks.name: Phillips curve / inflation-unemployment tradeoff
ticks.constraint: inflation and unemployment as independent policy variables
ticks.detail: A.W. Phillips found an empirical inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Policymakers thought they could choose a point on the curve. Friedman and Phelps showed (1968) the long-run curve is vertical — you can't permanently trade inflation for lower unemployment. The stagflation of the 1970s validated Friedman and ended Keynesian consensus.

links.label: Google Scholar: Phillips curve / inflation-unemployment tradeoff

ticks.name: Modigliani-Miller theorem / capital structure irrelevance
ticks.constraint: corporate capital structure (debt vs. equity mix) as a key value driver
ticks.detail: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller proved that in perfect markets, a company's value is independent of how it finances itself. Real-world deviations from their assumptions (taxes, bankruptcy costs, information asymmetry) explain actual capital structure choices. Every corporate finance decision since — buybacks, leverage, dividend policy — is analyzed against MM as a benchmark.

links.label: Wikipedia: Modigliani-Miller theorem / capital structure irrelevance
Google Scholar: Modigliani-Miller theorem / capital structure irrelevance

ticks.name: Market for lemons / information asymmetry (Akerlof)
ticks.constraint: markets as efficiently pricing quality when buyer and seller information differ
ticks.detail: George Akerlof's 'Market for Lemons' showed that when sellers know more than buyers about product quality, markets can collapse — buyers assume average quality, sellers with above-average products withdraw, quality falls, until only lemons remain. This explained used car markets, health insurance, and credit markets. Information economics, signaling theory, and market design all follow.

links.label: Wikipedia: Market for lemons / information asymmetry (Akerlof)
Google Scholar: Market for lemons / information asymmetry (Akerlof)

ticks.name: Black-Scholes / financial derivatives explosion
ticks.constraint: options pricing as requiring dealer intuition rather than mathematical formula
ticks.detail: The Black-Scholes-Merton formula priced options using only the current price, strike price, time to expiration, volatility, and interest rate. The derivatives market grew from $1 trillion to $1 quadrillion in notional value in 30 years. Also: the formula's assumption of continuous trading and normally distributed returns contributed to the 2008 financial crisis.

links.label: Google Scholar: Black-Scholes / financial derivatives explosion

ticks.name: Amazon.com / e-commerce and platform economics
ticks.constraint: retail transactions as requiring physical co-presence of buyer and seller
ticks.detail: Jeff Bezos started Amazon as an online bookstore in 1994. Within a decade it was everything. The click: e-commerce eliminated physical retail's geographic constraint. Long-tail economics (Chris Anderson) — the ability to stock and sell items that no physical store could afford to carry — restructured retail, publishing, music, and eventually every industry.

links.label: Wikipedia: Amazon.com / e-commerce and platform economics
Google Scholar: Amazon.com / e-commerce and platform economics

ticks.name: 2008 financial crisis / too-big-to-fail
ticks.constraint: systemic financial risk as manageable through market discipline alone
ticks.detail: The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered a global financial crisis that required unprecedented government bailouts. The tick: financial institutions had become so interconnected and large that their failure threatened the entire system — moral hazard at civilizational scale. Dodd-Frank, Basel III, and the entire post-crisis regulatory architecture responded to this.

ticks.name: First illustrated book (printed woodcuts)
ticks.constraint: illustrations in books as requiring individual hand copying
ticks.detail: The first books with printed woodcut illustrations (the Pfister Bible, ~1462) demonstrated that images could be mass-produced alongside text. Illustrated books transformed the transmission of scientific, botanical, anatomical, and geographical knowledge. Without printed images, Vesalius's anatomy, Fuchs's herbals, and Dürer's art prints couldn't have spread.

links.label: Google Scholar: First illustrated book (printed woodcuts)

ticks.name: Michelangelo's David / figural perfection
ticks.constraint: sculpture as constrained by available stone and religious subject
ticks.detail: David was carved from a single block of marble that had been considered unusable since 1463. Michelangelo's technical achievement — and his choice of the moment before action rather than the moment of triumph — redefined what sculpture could do. The nude male figure as an expression of humanist ideals rather than divine subject was the tick.

links.label: Google Scholar: Michelangelo's David / figural perfection

ticks.name: Dürer's woodcuts / printed art mass distribution
ticks.constraint: fine art as available only to those who could visit it
ticks.detail: Albrecht Dürer's mastery of woodcut and engraving printing allowed his works to circulate across Europe in editions of hundreds. The same image could be owned by a merchant in Antwerp and a scholar in Nuremberg. Printed art created an audience for visual culture that stretched far beyond the wealthy patron class. The art market as we know it begins here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Dürer's woodcuts / printed art mass distribution
Google Scholar: Dürer's woodcuts / printed art mass distribution

ticks.name: Baroque music / emotional expression in form
ticks.constraint: music as primarily liturgical or danced
ticks.detail: Claudio Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) — arguably the first opera — demonstrated that music could tell stories, convey psychological complexity, and express emotion as its primary purpose. The affetti (emotional states) became music's subject matter. From Baroque's emotional architecture to Classical's formal balance to Romantic's subjective intensity, Western art music developed from this shift.

links.label: Wikipedia: Baroque music / emotional expression in form
Google Scholar: Baroque music / emotional expression in form

ticks.name: First public opera house (Venice)
ticks.constraint: opera as entertainment limited to aristocratic courts
ticks.detail: The Teatro San Cassiano in Venice (1637) was the first opera house open to paying public audiences. Opera became a commercial art form for the first time. The economic model — tickets, star singers, impresarios — that financed Western classical music for 300 years was established here.

links.label: Google Scholar: First public opera house (Venice)

ticks.name: Antonio Stradivari / violin craft peak
ticks.constraint: string instrument quality as bounded by existing workshop knowledge
ticks.detail: Stradivari's violins (made 1666-1737) are still considered the finest ever made. His achievement codified what a violin could be — the geometry, thickness gradients, varnish, and wood selection that produce the instrument's characteristic tone. The instrument itself became a tick: it defined the sound that shaped Western music for 350 years.

links.label: Wikipedia: Antonio Stradivari / violin craft peak
Google Scholar: Antonio Stradivari / violin craft peak

ticks.name: Impressionism / painting en plein air
ticks.constraint: painting as a studio practice requiring stable conditions
ticks.detail: Monet, Renoir, and Sisley painted outdoors (en plein air) to capture light and atmosphere as they changed. The invention of portable tube paint (1841) made this possible. Impressionism shifted painting's subject from historical narrative and portraiture to perception itself — how light falls on a haystack at different times of day. Every subsequent modern art movement responds to Impressionism.

links.label: Wikipedia: Impressionism / painting en plein air
Google Scholar: Impressionism / painting en plein air

ticks.name: First film screening (Lumière, Paris)
ticks.constraint: photography as capturing a single moment
ticks.detail: The Lumières' first public screening at the Grand Café (December 28, 1895) showed L'Arrivée d'un train and workers leaving a factory. Moving pictures were a new medium. Within 20 years they had developed narrative grammar (editing, close-ups, camera movement), a global distribution system, and a star system. Cinema is the art form of the 20th century.

links.label: Google Scholar: First film screening (Lumière, Paris)

ticks.name: Armory Show / modernism arrives in America
ticks.constraint: American art as provincial relative to European tradition
ticks.detail: The 1913 International Exhibition of Modern Art in New York (the Armory Show) introduced American audiences to Cubism, Fauvism, and Post-Impressionism. Marcel Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase caused a scandal. American artists and collectors were changed. The US art world's trajectory from provincial to globally central began here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Armory Show / modernism arrives in America
Google Scholar: Armory Show / modernism arrives in America

ticks.name: Joyce's Ulysses / stream of consciousness novel
ticks.constraint: the novel as constrained to linear narrative and external description
ticks.detail: Ulysses mapped a single Dublin day through interior monologue, stream of consciousness, and a dozen different styles. The novel's subject became consciousness itself — its associative, fragmented, private quality. Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury, and the entire tradition of modernist fiction follow from Joyce's formal experiment.

links.label: Wikipedia: Joyce's Ulysses / stream of consciousness novel
Google Scholar: Joyce's Ulysses / stream of consciousness novel

ticks.name: Surrealism manifesto (Breton)
ticks.constraint: art as subject to rational control and conscious intention
ticks.detail: André Breton's Surrealist Manifesto declared that art should access the unconscious directly — automatic writing, dreamwork, and the irrational. Surrealism's imagery (Dalí's melting clocks, Magritte's impossible juxtapositions) created a visual language for the unconscious. Advertising, cinema, and political propaganda all learned from surrealism's techniques.

ticks.name: Abstract Expressionism / New York becomes art capital
ticks.constraint: European cities as the exclusive centers of contemporary art
ticks.detail: Pollock, de Kooning, Rothko, and Kline created a gestural, large-scale painting tradition that shifted the art world's center from Paris to New York. Abstract Expressionism was also shaped by CIA cultural diplomacy during the Cold War — it was promoted internationally as the art of a free society. The American art market's global dominance began here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Abstract Expressionism / New York becomes art capital
Google Scholar: Abstract Expressionism / New York becomes art capital

ticks.name: Pop Art / Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
ticks.constraint: the distinction between high art and commercial imagery
ticks.detail: Warhol's 1962 Campbell's Soup Cans exhibition made mass-produced consumer imagery the explicit subject of fine art. Pop Art erased the boundary between commerce and culture, between unique artworks and reproduction, between irony and celebration. The appropriation art, media criticism, and ironic sensibility of subsequent decades all begin with Warhol's silk-screens.

links.label: Wikipedia: Pop Art / Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
Google Scholar: Pop Art / Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans

ticks.name: Conceptual art / dematerialization
ticks.constraint: art as requiring a physical object
ticks.detail: Joseph Kosuth's 'One and Three Chairs' (a chair, a photograph of the chair, and a dictionary definition of 'chair') and Sol LeWitt's instructions-based works proposed that the concept is the art — the physical object is incidental. Conceptual art dematerialized the artwork. Performance art, installation art, and net art all follow from the tick that the idea is enough.

ticks.name: Punk rock / DIY cultural production
ticks.constraint: popular music production as requiring record label infrastructure
ticks.detail: The Ramones (1976) and the Sex Pistols (1977) demonstrated that you didn't need technical polish, extensive training, or a major label to record and perform music that connected. The 'anyone can do it' ethos of punk created the independent music ecosystem — indie labels, zines, DIY touring — that still exists as an alternative to the mainstream industry.

links.label: Wikipedia: Punk rock / DIY cultural production
Google Scholar: Punk rock / DIY cultural production

ticks.name: Hip hop / sampling as composition
ticks.constraint: music composition as requiring trained musicians playing original parts
ticks.detail: Grandmaster Flash's 'The Message' (1982) and Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock' established sampling — using fragments of existing recordings as the raw material for new compositions — as a legitimate musical practice. Sampling radically democratized music production and created a new compositional aesthetic built on quotation, reference, and recontextualization.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hip hop / sampling as composition
Google Scholar: Hip hop / sampling as composition

ticks.name: Mosaic browser / internet as publishing medium
ticks.constraint: publishing as requiring physical infrastructure (presses, distribution)
ticks.detail: The Web's graphical interface made self-publishing trivially easy. Blogs, webcomics, online journalism, and digital art emerged without gatekeepers. The long-tail economics of online distribution allowed niche creative work to find its audience globally. Every creator economy platform (YouTube, Substack, Bandcamp, Patreon) is a consequence of the Web's open publishing.

links.label: Wikipedia: Mosaic browser / internet as publishing medium
Google Scholar: Mosaic browser / internet as publishing medium

ticks.name: YouTube / video democratized
ticks.constraint: video production and distribution as requiring broadcast infrastructure
ticks.detail: YouTube's 'Broadcast Yourself' (2005) made video publishing free and global. Within years, YouTube creators had audiences larger than network television. The entire creator economy — tutorials, vlogs, independent journalism, music videos, long-form documentary — migrated online. Traditional broadcast's gatekeeping role effectively ended for a generation of creators.

ticks.name: DALL-E / Midjourney / AI image generation
ticks.constraint: visual creation requiring either artistic skill or professional production
ticks.detail: Text-to-image AI systems (DALL-E 2, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion) let anyone describe an image and receive a high-quality generated result. The economic impact on stock photography, illustration, and concept art was immediate. The aesthetic impact — a new visual language trained on all human imagery — is still emerging. What it means for human authorship and creativity is unresolved.

links.label: Ramesh et al. — DALL-E: Zero-Shot Text-to-Image Generation (2021)
MIT Technology Review: The text-to-image revolution

ticks.name: Ada Lovelace / first algorithm
ticks.constraint: computation as purely numerical — not capable of manipulating symbols
ticks.detail: Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine include what is recognized as the first algorithm intended for machine execution — instructions for computing Bernoulli numbers. She also articulated the possibility that the Engine could manipulate symbols beyond numbers. The first vision of general-purpose computing as symbol manipulation, not just arithmetic.

links.label: Google Scholar: Ada Lovelace / first algorithm

ticks.name: Hollerith tabulating machine / US Census
ticks.constraint: census data processing as requiring years of manual calculation
ticks.detail: Herman Hollerith's punch-card tabulating machine completed the 1890 US Census in one year (vs. eight years for 1880). The machine became the foundation of IBM. Punch-card data processing dominated computing until the 1970s. The idea that data could be mechanically sorted and counted — not just stored — was the tick.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hollerith tabulating machine / US Census
Google Scholar: Hollerith tabulating machine / US Census

ticks.name: Turing's computability / halting problem
ticks.constraint: the limits of what machines can compute as unknown
ticks.detail: Alongside proposing the universal machine, Turing proved the halting problem undecidable — no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program will ever stop running. This established fundamental limits on what computation can achieve. Computer science's theory of computability — what problems are algorithmically solvable — is built on this proof.

links.label: Google Scholar: Turing's computability / halting problem

ticks.name: ENIAC / first general-purpose electronic computer
ticks.constraint: programmable computation as requiring mechanical or electromechanical components
ticks.detail: ENIAC used 18,000 vacuum tubes and could perform 5,000 additions per second — 1,000x faster than existing electromechanical computers. It was programmed by physically rewiring the machine. The first electronic computer demonstrated the paradigm that electronic switching could compute at speeds no mechanical device could approach.

links.label: Wikipedia: ENIAC / first general-purpose electronic computer
Google Scholar: ENIAC / first general-purpose electronic computer

ticks.name: Transistor (Bell Labs, Shockley/Bardeen/Brattain)
ticks.constraint: electronic switching requiring fragile, hot, power-hungry vacuum tubes
ticks.detail: The transistor replaced the vacuum tube as the basic electronic switching element. It was smaller, cooler, more reliable, and faster. The integrated circuit, the microprocessor, and modern computing are all transistors at varying scales. Shockley's subsequent founding of Fairchild Semiconductor launched Silicon Valley.

ticks.name: FORTRAN / first high-level programming language
ticks.constraint: programming requiring direct instruction in machine code or assembly
ticks.detail: IBM's FORTRAN (1957) was the first compiled high-level language — programmers wrote mathematical formulas that a compiler translated into machine code. The productivity gain was 10-20x. COBOL (1959) followed for business. Every programming language since — C, Python, Java, JavaScript — descends from the concept FORTRAN established.

links.label: Wikipedia: FORTRAN / first high-level programming language
Google Scholar: FORTRAN / first high-level programming language

ticks.name: Time-sharing / interactive computing (McCarthy)
ticks.constraint: computers as batch-processing machines serving one job at a time
ticks.detail: John McCarthy's time-sharing proposal (1959) and its implementation at MIT showed that a single computer could serve multiple users simultaneously by rapidly switching between them. Interactive computing — the ability to type a command and immediately get a response — transformed how computers were used. The terminal, the command line, and eventually the GUI all require time-sharing.

ticks.name: Moore's Law observed
ticks.constraint: computing cost as a fixed rather than exponentially declining parameter
ticks.detail: Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling approximately every two years (later standardized to 18 months). His prediction became a self-fulfilling prophecy that organized the entire semiconductor industry's roadmap for 50 years. Moore's Law is why a 2024 smartphone has more computing power than 1990's entire world combined.

ticks.name: Doug Engelbart's Mother of All Demos
ticks.constraint: computing as batch processing of text — not interactive visual manipulation
ticks.detail: Engelbart's December 9, 1968 demonstration showed the mouse, hypertext, videoconferencing, collaborative editing, and windowed interfaces — essentially previewing the modern PC. All of it was working software. The demo defined the trajectory of personal computing. Steve Jobs cited it as inspiration for the Macintosh. Every GUI computer interface today is Engelbart's vision.

links.label: Wikipedia: Doug Engelbart's Mother of All Demos
Google Scholar: Doug Engelbart's Mother of All Demos

ticks.name: C programming language (Ritchie)
ticks.constraint: systems programming as requiring assembly language
ticks.detail: Dennis Ritchie's C language allowed operating systems and low-level software to be written in a portable, human-readable language rather than machine-specific assembly code. Unix was rewritten in C (1973). Every major operating system — Linux, macOS, Windows — is still primarily written in C or languages derived from it. Python, Java, and JavaScript all run on C-based runtimes.

ticks.name: Ethernet / local area networking (Metcalfe)
ticks.constraint: computers as isolated islands unable to share resources
ticks.detail: Robert Metcalfe's Ethernet (1973, standardized 1980) connected computers within a building into a local area network. Files, printers, and eventually the internet could be shared. Metcalfe's Law: the value of a network is proportional to the square of its connected users. Every office network, home router, and cloud data center uses Ethernet.

links.label: Google Scholar: Ethernet / local area networking (Metcalfe)

ticks.name: VisiCalc and the business computer revolution
ticks.constraint: business computing as requiring mainframe infrastructure and IT departments
ticks.detail: VisiCalc on the Apple II (1979) and then Lotus 1-2-3 on the IBM PC (1983) made personal computers indispensable business tools. CFOs and executives adopted personal computers for financial modeling — the 'killer app' that justified the hardware purchase. The spreadsheet is still the most widely used business software, 45 years later.

links.label: Wikipedia: VisiCalc and the business computer revolution
Google Scholar: VisiCalc and the business computer revolution

ticks.name: Macintosh / graphical user interface for everyone
ticks.constraint: personal computing as requiring command-line expertise
ticks.detail: The 1984 Macintosh brought the graphical user interface — windows, icons, mouse, pointer — to a mass market at an affordable price. It made computing visual, spatial, and manipulable rather than textual and memorized. The Mac didn't invent the GUI (Xerox PARC did, Engelbart before that) but it commercialized it. Windows followed. The command line receded.

links.label: Wikipedia: Macintosh / graphical user interface for everyone
Google Scholar: Macintosh / graphical user interface for everyone

ticks.name: World Wide Web (Berners-Lee) protocols
ticks.constraint: internet as requiring technical knowledge to navigate
ticks.detail: Berners-Lee's HTTP, HTML, and URL proposals (1989-1991) created the Web as a system of linked documents that any program (browser) could navigate. The Web was built on the internet but made it accessible. By 1993 (Mosaic), anyone could browse it. By 1995 (Netscape), it was transforming commerce, media, and communication.

links.label: Google Scholar: World Wide Web (Berners-Lee) protocols

ticks.name: JavaScript / browser programming
ticks.constraint: web pages as static documents that only servers could change
ticks.detail: Brendan Eich created JavaScript in 10 days at Netscape in 1995. It allowed web pages to respond to user interactions without reloading. The dynamic, interactive web — Gmail, Google Maps, Facebook, every modern web application — runs on JavaScript. It's the most widely deployed programming language in history, despite Eich's own ambivalence about it.

ticks.name: Google PageRank / search at scale
ticks.constraint: web search as keyword-matching without relevance ranking
ticks.detail: Larry Page and Sergey Brin's PageRank algorithm ranked pages by the number and quality of links pointing to them. It made search useful for the first time. Google's dominance — and the entire SEO industry — followed. The Web became navigable. Knowledge that previously required visiting a library became accessible in seconds.

links.label: Wikipedia: Google PageRank / search at scale
Google Scholar: Google PageRank / search at scale

ticks.name: Facebook's News Feed / algorithmic social curation
ticks.constraint: social media feeds as chronological and user-curated
ticks.detail: Facebook's News Feed (2006) introduced algorithmic curation — a proprietary algorithm deciding what each user sees based on engagement predictions. Twitter, Instagram, TikTok all followed with increasingly sophisticated algorithmic feeds. The tick: attention became a product, algorithmically optimized. The downstream effects on democracy, mental health, and public discourse are still being assessed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Facebook's News Feed / algorithmic social curation
Google Scholar: Facebook's News Feed / algorithmic social curation

ticks.name: iPhone's App Store model / platform economics
ticks.constraint: software distribution as requiring physical media or complex installation
ticks.detail: Apple's App Store (2008) created the first large-scale app marketplace with standardized discovery, payment, and distribution. A single developer could reach hundreds of millions of users. Platform economics — the 30% developer cut that Apple and Google take — became the defining business model of the mobile era. Antitrust regulators are still arguing about whether it's legal.

links.label: Wikipedia: iPhone's App Store model / platform economics
Google Scholar: iPhone's App Store model / platform economics

ticks.name: GitHub / distributed version control
ticks.constraint: collaborative software development requiring a central authoritative server
ticks.detail: GitHub (2008) built a social layer on top of Git (Linus Torvalds' distributed version control system, 2005). Open-source collaboration became frictionless — fork a project, make changes, propose a merge. Every major open-source project (Linux, Python, TensorFlow) is now developed on GitHub. Microsoft acquired it for $7.5B in 2018.

links.label: Google Scholar: GitHub / distributed version control

ticks.name: Kubernetes / container orchestration
ticks.constraint: cloud application deployment as requiring custom infrastructure configuration
ticks.detail: Google's Kubernetes (2014) automated the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Docker containers + Kubernetes orchestration became the standard way to run cloud-native applications. Every major cloud provider, every large-scale web application, and the AI inference infrastructure running LLMs today uses Kubernetes.

ticks.name: Gregorian calendar reform
ticks.constraint: calendar drift from solar year accumulating to 10+ days
ticks.detail: Pope Gregory XIII's reform corrected the Julian calendar's 11-minute annual error — which had accumulated to 10 days by 1582. The solution: skip leap year in century years not divisible by 400. The Gregorian calendar coordinates global timekeeping, agriculture, religious observance, and international business. Adopted progressively: Britain 1752, Russia 1918, China 1912.

ticks.name: Reflecting telescope (Newton)
ticks.constraint: refracting telescopes' chromatic aberration limiting magnification
ticks.detail: Newton's reflecting telescope used a curved mirror instead of a lens, eliminating chromatic aberration that blurred images in refracting telescopes. Larger, more powerful telescopes became possible. The Hubble Space Telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope, and all major modern observatories use reflecting optics. Newton's design is essentially unchanged.

ticks.name: Rømer measures speed of light
ticks.constraint: light as instantaneously propagating
ticks.detail: Ole Rømer noticed that Jupiter's moon Io appeared to orbit slightly faster when Earth moved toward Jupiter and slower when moving away — explaining the discrepancy by the finite travel time of light. The first measurement of the speed of light (within 25% of the correct value). It proved light has a finite speed and opened the question of what light travels through.

links.label: Wikipedia: Rømer measures speed of light
Google Scholar: Rømer measures speed of light

ticks.name: Oersted / electromagnetism connection
ticks.constraint: electricity and magnetism as separate phenomena
