ticks.detail: Hans Christian Oersted accidentally noticed that a compass needle deflected when placed near a current-carrying wire. Electricity could create magnetism. Faraday showed magnetism could create electricity. Maxwell unified both in his equations. The entire technology of electric motors, generators, radio, and wireless communication follows from Oersted's lecture-table accident.

ticks.name: Maxwell's equations / unified electromagnetism
ticks.constraint: electricity, magnetism, and light as separate phenomena
ticks.detail: James Clerk Maxwell's four equations unified electricity and magnetism into a single theory and predicted electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light — implying that light IS an electromagnetic wave. Radio, radar, microwave, X-ray, UV, and all of the electromagnetic spectrum follow from Maxwell. Einstein said Maxwell's equations were 'the most profound and the most fruitful that physics has experienced since Newton.'

links.label: Google Scholar: Maxwell's equations / unified electromagnetism

ticks.name: Electron discovered (Thomson)
ticks.constraint: the atom as the fundamental, indivisible unit of matter
ticks.detail: J.J. Thomson's cathode ray experiments identified the electron — a particle far smaller than any atom, with negative charge. Atoms had sub-atomic structure. The atom was not the bottom of the ladder. Thomson proposed the 'plum pudding' model. Rutherford's 1911 nuclear model replaced it. The entire 20th century nuclear physics program begins with this discovery.

ticks.name: Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom
ticks.constraint: the atom as a uniformly distributed charge (Thomson's plum pudding)
ticks.detail: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed that most of an atom's mass is concentrated in a tiny, dense, positively-charged nucleus. The atom is mostly empty space. This nuclear model — a dense nucleus orbited by electrons — is still the mental model most people use. It directly enabled nuclear physics, the neutron discovery, and nuclear fission.

links.label: Wikipedia: Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom
Google Scholar: Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom

ticks.name: General relativity (Einstein)
ticks.constraint: gravity as a force acting across empty space
ticks.detail: General relativity replaced Newton's gravitational force with the geometry of curved spacetime — mass tells spacetime how to curve, curved spacetime tells mass how to move. Confirmed by the 1919 solar eclipse (light bending around the sun). GPS satellites require general relativistic corrections. Black holes, gravitational waves, the expanding universe, and cosmology all require GR.

ticks.name: Hubble's law / expanding universe
ticks.constraint: the universe as static and eternal
ticks.detail: Edwin Hubble's observation that galaxies are receding at velocities proportional to their distance proved the universe is expanding. Running the film backward implies a beginning — the Big Bang. Cosmology as a quantitative science was born. The CMB (1965), dark energy (1998), and the entire narrative of cosmic history all follow from Hubble's observation.

links.label: Google Scholar: Hubble's law / expanding universe

ticks.name: Cyclotron / particle accelerator (Lawrence)
ticks.constraint: particle physics limited to natural cosmic ray energies
ticks.detail: Ernest Lawrence's cyclotron (1932) used magnetic fields to spiral charged particles to high energies. Artificial particle acceleration allowed physicists to probe nuclear and subnuclear structure at will. The technology scaled from Lawrence's 27cm device to CERN's 27km LHC. Every fundamental particle discovery since the neutron used accelerator technology.

ticks.name: Nuclear fission (Hahn and Strassmann / Meitner)
ticks.constraint: atomic energy as inaccessibly small-scale
ticks.detail: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann showed that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium — the uranium nucleus had split. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch correctly identified this as fission and calculated the energy released (E=mc²). From discovery to atomic bomb was 7 years. From discovery to nuclear power was 20. From discovery to modern civilization's energy mix is still ongoing.

links.label: Wikipedia: Nuclear fission (Hahn and Strassmann / Meitner)
Google Scholar: Nuclear fission (Hahn and Strassmann / Meitner)

ticks.name: Cosmic microwave background discovered (Penzias/Wilson)
ticks.constraint: the Big Bang as a theoretical framework without direct observational evidence
ticks.detail: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, while trying to eliminate interference from their antenna, discovered a faint, uniform microwave radiation coming from all directions — the afterglow of the Big Bang. The CMB confirmed the Big Bang theory definitively. Subsequent CMB measurements (COBE, WMAP, Planck) have mapped the early universe with extraordinary precision.

links.label: Google Scholar: Cosmic microwave background discovered (Penzias/Wilson)

ticks.name: Dark energy discovered (Type Ia supernovae)
ticks.constraint: the universe's expansion as decelerating due to gravity
ticks.detail: Two independent teams observed that distant Type Ia supernovae were dimmer than expected — the universe's expansion was accelerating, not decelerating. Something (dark energy) was pushing the universe apart against gravity. Dark energy constitutes 68% of the universe's energy content. Its nature is completely unknown. The Standard Model of cosmology required fundamental revision.

links.label: Wikipedia: Dark energy discovered (Type Ia supernovae)
Google Scholar: Dark energy discovered (Type Ia supernovae)

ticks.name: First image of a black hole (Event Horizon Telescope)
ticks.constraint: black holes as theoretically inevitable but photographically inaccessible
ticks.detail: The Event Horizon Telescope linked radio telescopes across Earth to create an Earth-sized interferometer. The resulting image of M87*'s shadow — the first direct visual evidence of a black hole's event horizon — matched general relativity's predictions exactly. A century after Einstein predicted black holes, humanity photographed one.

links.label: Wikipedia: First image of a black hole (Event Horizon Telescope)
Google Scholar: First image of a black hole (Event Horizon Telescope)

ticks.name: Twelve Tables / Rome's first written law
ticks.constraint: Roman law as oral, customary, and known only to patricians
ticks.detail: The Twelve Tables, displayed publicly in the Forum, made Roman law accessible to plebeians for the first time. Written law that citizens could consult and cite changed the balance of power between social classes. The principle that law must be written and public — not the private knowledge of a privileged class — underlies every subsequent legal system.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twelve Tables / Rome's first written law
Google Scholar: Twelve Tables / Rome's first written law

ticks.name: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis / Roman law codified
ticks.constraint: Roman legal tradition as fragmented across thousands of incompatible texts
ticks.detail: Emperor Justinian commissioned the systematic compilation and codification of Roman law — the Institutes, Digest, Code, and Novels. The Corpus became the foundation of civil law systems across continental Europe, Latin America, and parts of Asia. Every French, Spanish, Italian, German, and Brazilian legal system traces to Justinian's codification.

links.label: Wikipedia: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis / Roman law codified
Google Scholar: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis / Roman law codified

ticks.name: Magna Carta / limits on sovereign power
ticks.constraint: the monarch's discretion as the supreme law
ticks.detail: The 39th clause — 'No free man shall be seized, imprisoned, dispossessed, outlawed, exiled, or ruined in any way, except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land' — is the seed of habeas corpus, due process, and constitutional government. Magna Carta's symbolic importance exceeds its actual 1215 provisions.

links.label: Wikipedia: Magna Carta / limits on sovereign power
Google Scholar: Magna Carta / limits on sovereign power

ticks.name: English Bill of Rights / constitutional monarchy
ticks.constraint: English monarchy as absolute following Stuart restoration
ticks.detail: The Bill of Rights formalized the Glorious Revolution's settlement: parliamentary supremacy, free elections, free speech in Parliament, no excessive bail, no standing army in peacetime without Parliamentary consent. England became a constitutional monarchy. The American Bill of Rights is modeled directly on it.

links.label: Wikipedia: English Bill of Rights / constitutional monarchy
Google Scholar: English Bill of Rights / constitutional monarchy

ticks.name: US Bill of Rights / individual rights against state
ticks.constraint: constitutional government as silent on individual liberties
ticks.detail: The first ten amendments to the US Constitution enumerated specific protections: free speech, free press, freedom of religion, right to bear arms, protection from unreasonable search, right to a fair trial, prohibition of cruel punishment. The concept of enumerated individual rights against government became the model for constitutional rights globally.

links.label: Wikipedia: US Bill of Rights / individual rights against state
Google Scholar: US Bill of Rights / individual rights against state

ticks.name: International humanitarian law (Lieber Code)
ticks.constraint: treatment of prisoners and civilians in war as entirely discretionary
ticks.detail: Francis Lieber's Instructions for the Government of Armies of the United States in the Field (1863) was the first codification of the laws of land warfare. It prohibited torture of prisoners, protection of civilians, and destruction of property beyond military necessity. It directly influenced the Hague Conventions (1899, 1907) and the Geneva Conventions.

links.label: Google Scholar: International humanitarian law (Lieber Code)

ticks.name: League of Nations Covenant / collective security
ticks.constraint: international dispute resolution as purely bilateral negotiation or war
ticks.detail: The League Covenant created the first multilateral dispute resolution mechanism with collective security obligations. It failed — but the institutional form it invented (permanent secretariat, regular assembly, arbitration procedures) was refined by the UN. International organizations as permanent institutions with their own legal personality begin here.

links.label: Wikipedia: League of Nations Covenant / collective security
Google Scholar: League of Nations Covenant / collective security

ticks.name: UN Charter / sovereign equality principle
ticks.constraint: international order as based on power hierarchy rather than legal equality
ticks.detail: The UN Charter's assertion that all member states are sovereign equals — regardless of size, power, or wealth — created a legal fiction that nonetheless structured international relations. Every state has one vote in the General Assembly. The veto in the Security Council was the concession to power reality. The tension between sovereign equality and great-power politics continues.

links.label: Wikipedia: UN Charter / sovereign equality principle
Google Scholar: UN Charter / sovereign equality principle

ticks.name: Genocide Convention / defining a new crime
ticks.constraint: the systematic destruction of an ethnic or national group as legally unnamed
ticks.detail: Raphael Lemkin coined 'genocide' in 1944 and the Convention criminalizing it was adopted in 1948. For the first time, the systematic destruction of a group based on ethnicity, nationality, race, or religion was defined as a crime under international law. The enforcement gap (Rwanda, Srebrenica) showed the definition's power and its limits.

links.label: Wikipedia: Genocide Convention / defining a new crime
Google Scholar: Genocide Convention / defining a new crime

ticks.name: European Convention on Human Rights
ticks.constraint: human rights as aspirational declarations without enforcement
ticks.detail: The ECHR created the European Court of Human Rights — the first international court with compulsory jurisdiction over human rights cases, where individuals could bring claims against their own governments. Human rights became enforceable law, not just rhetoric. The template for regional human rights systems worldwide.

links.label: Wikipedia: European Convention on Human Rights
Google Scholar: European Convention on Human Rights

ticks.name: Amnesty International founded / human rights NGOs
ticks.constraint: human rights monitoring as requiring state cooperation
ticks.detail: Peter Benenson's Observer article 'The Forgotten Prisoners' (1961) launched Amnesty International — an NGO that independently documented and publicized human rights abuses regardless of which government committed them. Non-governmental human rights monitoring created accountability pressure outside diplomatic channels. Human Rights Watch, ACLU, and every human rights NGO follows this model.

links.label: Wikipedia: Amnesty International founded / human rights NGOs
Google Scholar: Amnesty International founded / human rights NGOs

ticks.name: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda
ticks.constraint: genocide as politically prosecutable only domestically by perpetrators' own government
ticks.detail: The ICTR was the first international tribunal to convict for genocide since Nuremberg. It established that genocide can be prosecuted internationally even against sitting heads of state. The International Criminal Court (2002) built directly on the ICTR and the ICTY (Yugoslavia tribunal) experience.

links.label: Wikipedia: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda
Google Scholar: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda

ticks.name: GDPR / right to digital privacy as law
ticks.constraint: personal data as freely usable by those who collected it
ticks.detail: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation came into force in May 2018 — the most comprehensive privacy law in history. It gave Europeans rights over their personal data: the right to access, correct, delete, and port it. It imposed fines up to 4% of global revenue. Every tech company's privacy policy globally changed because of GDPR. It established digital privacy as a legal right.

links.label: Wikipedia: GDPR / right to digital privacy as law
Google Scholar: GDPR / right to digital privacy as law

ticks.name: Proto-cuneiform accounting tokens
ticks.constraint: commercial record-keeping as dependent on human memory alone
ticks.detail: Before writing proper, Mesopotamian merchants used clay tokens of various shapes to represent different commodities — 3 cones for wheat, 2 discs for oil. These accounting tokens are the immediate precursor to cuneiform writing. The click: externalizing memory into physical objects that outlast the transaction. Writing was invented for commerce, not literature.

ticks.name: Ugaritic alphabet / simplified writing
ticks.constraint: Phoenician consonantal script as limited to Semitic languages
ticks.detail: The Ugaritic alphabet (1400 BC) was the first alphabetic script adapted for writing on clay tablets in cuneiform-style wedges — combining the simplicity of an alphabet with the durability of cuneiform. It accelerated the development of alphabetic writing as the dominant script technology across the Near East, eventually displacing syllabic scripts everywhere.

links.label: Google Scholar: Ugaritic alphabet / simplified writing

ticks.name: Papyrus scrolls / lightweight portable writing surface
ticks.constraint: writing as requiring heavy clay tablets or expensive parchment
ticks.detail: Papyrus — the pressed pith of the Cyperus papyrus plant — provided a lightweight, flexible writing surface that allowed document portability impossible with clay. Egyptian civilization's administrative correspondence, the Alexandrian Library, and the transmission of Greek philosophy all depended on papyrus. It made long-distance textual communication routine.

links.label: Wikipedia: Papyrus scrolls / lightweight portable writing surface
Google Scholar: Papyrus scrolls / lightweight portable writing surface

ticks.name: Arabic as global language of science
ticks.constraint: scientific and philosophical knowledge as accessible only in Greek or Latin
ticks.detail: From 800-1200 AD, Arabic was the dominant language of natural philosophy, mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad translated Greek texts into Arabic and extended them significantly. When Europeans sought ancient knowledge, they learned Arabic to access it. Scientific vocabulary in European languages (algebra, algorithm, almanac, alcohol, zenith) is Arabic because Arabic was the language of science.

links.label: Wikipedia: Arabic as global language of science
Google Scholar: Arabic as global language of science

ticks.name: Gutenberg / text becomes reproducible
ticks.constraint: text as unique — each copy individually produced
ticks.detail: The printing press made text reproducible and identical. Before Gutenberg, each manuscript copy introduced errors and variations. After: the identical edition. Scholars could cite specific pages. Scientific priority could be established. The edition — a specific text at a specific moment — became the basic unit of written culture. Error correction, bibliographic control, and academic citation systems all follow.

links.label: Google Scholar: Gutenberg / text becomes reproducible

ticks.name: Académie Française / standardized language
ticks.constraint: national language as dialectally fragmented and without authoritative standard
ticks.detail: Richelieu's Académie Française was established to standardize and purify the French language. The idea that a language could be institutionally governed — its vocabulary regulated, its grammar codified, its 'correct' usage enforced — was new. National language standardization became a European project: the Dictionary of the English Language (Johnson, 1755), Grimm's Deutsches Wörterbuch. Language as a national institution.

links.label: Google Scholar: Académie Française / standardized language

ticks.name: Johnson's Dictionary / lexicography standardized
ticks.constraint: English vocabulary as undefined, inconsistently spelled, and authority-less
ticks.detail: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary (1755) standardized English spelling, defined words with precision and illustrative quotations, and established the dictionary as an authoritative reference. Johnson's self-deprecating definition of lexicographer ('a writer of dictionaries, a harmless drudge') didn't diminish its impact. Every English dictionary since builds on Johnson's methodology.

links.label: Google Scholar: Johnson's Dictionary / lexicography standardized

ticks.name: Champollion / Rosetta Stone decoded
ticks.constraint: ancient Egyptian writing as permanently undecipherable
ticks.detail: Jean-François Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphics (1822) using the Rosetta Stone unlocked 3,500 years of Egyptian writing that had been opaque for 1,400 years. The method — parallel text as the key — became the template for deciphering other lost scripts. Mayan glyphs were similarly cracked in the 1990s using the same approach.

links.label: Google Scholar: Champollion / Rosetta Stone decoded

ticks.name: International Phonetic Alphabet
ticks.constraint: language transcription as varying incompatibly across different national traditions
ticks.detail: The International Phonetic Alphabet (1888) provided a standardized system for transcribing any human speech sound using a consistent set of symbols. Linguists could describe any language's sounds precisely. Language documentation, foreign language teaching, speech therapy, and computational linguistics all use the IPA. Every language's pronunciation can now be precisely recorded.

ticks.name: Saussure / synchronic linguistics
ticks.constraint: linguistics as exclusively historical (how languages changed over time)
ticks.detail: Saussure distinguished synchronic linguistics (studying a language at a single moment) from diachronic (historical). He argued the synchronic perspective — language as a system of relationships — was the more fundamental. Structural linguistics, which analyzed language as a system rather than as historical development, dominates 20th-century linguistics.

ticks.name: Machine translation first attempts (Weaver memo)
ticks.constraint: translation as requiring human linguistic knowledge
ticks.detail: Warren Weaver's 1949 memo proposed using computers for translation, analogizing it to cryptography — finding the 'code' underlying natural language. The first MT systems emerged in the 1950s, overpromising and underdelivering. But the research program established NLP as a field. Statistical MT (1990s), neural MT (2016), and LLM-based translation (2020s) all trace to Weaver's memo.

links.label: Wikipedia: Machine translation first attempts (Weaver memo)
Google Scholar: Machine translation first attempts (Weaver memo)

ticks.name: Chomsky / universal grammar hypothesis
ticks.constraint: human language as infinitely diverse and mutually incomparable
ticks.detail: Chomsky proposed that all human languages share deep structural properties — a universal grammar — which is biologically innate. Language acquisition is not imitation learning but the triggering of an innate capacity. This positioned linguistics within cognitive science and biology. The debate about what is universal and what is culturally specific in language continues.

links.label: Google Scholar: Chomsky / universal grammar hypothesis

ticks.name: Unicode / global character encoding
ticks.constraint: digital text as representable only in ASCII's 128 Roman-alphabet characters
ticks.detail: Unicode (1991, expanded through the 1990s) created a universal encoding standard for every character in every human language — over 140,000 characters across 150+ scripts. Before Unicode, every language required its own incompatible encoding system. After: a single Chinese, Arabic, or emoji character could be transmitted and displayed anywhere. The global internet became multilingual.

links.label: Google Scholar: Unicode / global character encoding

ticks.name: Twitter / microblogging and public real-time discourse
ticks.constraint: public written discourse as requiring editorial infrastructure
ticks.detail: Twitter's 140-character limit (later 280) created a new form: the public microblog. Real-time commentary on events, direct access to public figures, and a global shared timeline emerged. The Arab Spring, #MeToo, and the 2016 election were all Twitter-shaped phenomena. The character limit was a design constraint that became an aesthetic and a genre.

links.label: Wikipedia: Twitter / microblogging and public real-time discourse
Google Scholar: Twitter / microblogging and public real-time discourse

ticks.name: Hippocratic corpus / natural disease causation
ticks.constraint: disease as caused by divine punishment or demonic possession
ticks.detail: The Hippocratic school (5th century BC) rejected supernatural explanations for disease systematically for the first time. 'Sacred disease' (epilepsy) was caused by the brain, not the gods. Natural causes, clinical observation, prognosis, and diet became medicine's tools. The Hippocratic Oath established medical ethics. Western medicine's naturalistic tradition begins here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hippocratic corpus / natural disease causation
Google Scholar: Hippocratic corpus / natural disease causation

ticks.name: Galen's medical synthesis
ticks.constraint: Greek and Roman medical knowledge as fragmented across competing schools
ticks.detail: Claudius Galen systematized Greek medical knowledge into a comprehensive framework that dominated Western medicine for 1,400 years. His errors (blood is made in the liver; arteries carry air) were as consequential as his insights. Medicine couldn't advance until Vesalius (1543) and Harvey (1628) dismantled Galen — showing how a wrong authoritative synthesis can block progress.

ticks.name: Al-Zahrawi / surgical instruments and techniques
ticks.constraint: surgery as undocumented craft knowledge passed informally
ticks.detail: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi's Kitab al-Tasrif included the first illustrated surgical encyclopedia — describing over 200 surgical instruments, many of which he invented. Ligature of blood vessels, catgut sutures, and surgical treatment of cancer were documented. European surgery through the Renaissance drew heavily on Al-Zahrawi's translations.

links.label: Wikipedia: Al-Zahrawi / surgical instruments and techniques
Google Scholar: Al-Zahrawi / surgical instruments and techniques

ticks.name: Black Death / quarantine invented
ticks.constraint: epidemic disease spread as unstoppable once it reached a port city
ticks.detail: Venice's 1377 law requiring ships from infected ports to anchor for 30 days (later 40 — quarantine from 'quarantina giorni') was the first systematic epidemic containment measure. Quarantine proved partially effective against the plague and was adopted across Mediterranean ports. Every subsequent epidemic response — COVID-19 lockdowns included — descends from Venice's 1377 law.

links.label: Google Scholar: Black Death / quarantine invented

ticks.name: Vesalius / human anatomy through direct observation
ticks.constraint: anatomy as knowable through Galen's texts without direct observation
ticks.detail: De Humani Corporis Fabrica established that anatomy must be learned by dissecting actual human bodies, not by reading ancient texts. Vesalius corrected over 200 of Galen's errors. The principle that direct observation supersedes authority — not just in anatomy but in all of medicine — makes Vesalius foundational to scientific medicine.

links.label: Wikipedia: Vesalius / human anatomy through direct observation
Google Scholar: Vesalius / human anatomy through direct observation

ticks.name: Jenner's smallpox vaccination
ticks.constraint: smallpox as an unavoidable risk of existence requiring only prayer or variolation
ticks.detail: Edward Jenner's cowpox inoculation against smallpox was not the first vaccination attempt — variolation (deliberately infecting with mild smallpox) was practiced in Turkey and China for centuries. But Jenner's systematic demonstration that a related virus could confer immunity without disease risk was the tick. The principle of vaccination — training immunity with harmless antigens — follows from Jenner.

ticks.name: Crawford Long / first use of ether in surgery
ticks.constraint: surgical pain as an unavoidable feature of any operation
ticks.detail: Crawford Long removed a neck tumor from James Venable under ether anesthesia in Jefferson, Georgia in 1842 — four years before Morton's public Boston demonstration. Long didn't publish. The tick of surgical anesthesia was independently achieved and publicly demonstrated by multiple people within years of each other. The concept was ready; the first systematic demonstration mattered.

links.label: Wikipedia: Crawford Long / first use of ether in surgery
Google Scholar: Crawford Long / first use of ether in surgery

ticks.name: John Snow / cholera and epidemiology
ticks.constraint: cholera as transmitted by miasma (bad air)
ticks.detail: John Snow's mapping of cholera cases around the Broad Street pump during London's 1854 epidemic — and his removal of the pump handle — was the founding act of modern epidemiology. He proved cholera was waterborne before germ theory explained how. The detective work of tracing disease to a source — the epidemiological method — begins here.

links.label: Wikipedia: John Snow / cholera and epidemiology
Google Scholar: John Snow / cholera and epidemiology

ticks.name: X-ray diagnosis (first clinical use)
ticks.constraint: internal structures as visible only after death or major surgery
ticks.detail: Within weeks of Röntgen's November 1895 discovery, X-rays were being used clinically — imaging broken bones, foreign objects, and lung disease. The first radiograph of a living hand (Röntgen's wife, Anna Bertha Ludwig) showed the skeleton and a wedding ring. Diagnostic medicine was fundamentally changed — the body became transparent to investigation without surgery.

links.label: Google Scholar: X-ray diagnosis (first clinical use)

ticks.name: Insulin treatment of diabetes
ticks.constraint: type 1 diabetes as invariably fatal within months of diagnosis
ticks.detail: Before insulin, patients with type 1 diabetes were placed on starvation diets that extended life by months. Banting and Best's 1921 extraction of insulin from dog pancreas, first used in Leonard Thompson in January 1922, reversed the death sentence. Within a year, insulin was being manufactured industrially. The most immediate life-saving pharmaceutical discovery in history.

links.label: Google Scholar: Insulin treatment of diabetes

ticks.name: Sulfonamide drugs / first antibacterials
ticks.constraint: bacterial infection as untreatable by any pharmacological agent
ticks.detail: Gerhard Domagk discovered Prontosil's antibacterial effect in 1932 — the first sulfonamide drug. It was the first antibacterial effective enough to use clinically, saving lives from puerperal fever, pneumonia, and meningitis before penicillin. FDR's son's life was saved by sulfonamides in 1936, accelerating US adoption. They transformed infectious disease medicine before penicillin arrived.

links.label: Google Scholar: Sulfonamide drugs / first antibacterials

ticks.name: Kidney dialysis machine (Kolff)
ticks.constraint: renal failure as invariably fatal
ticks.detail: Willem Kolff built the first kidney dialysis machine from orange juice cans and cellophane sausage casings in Nazi-occupied Netherlands. His first 16 patients died; the 17th survived. Dialysis created the concept of artificial organ replacement — a machine that could substitute for a failing biological organ. Every form of organ support technology (ECMO, ventricular assist devices) follows Kolff's principle.

ticks.name: Coronary artery bypass surgery (Favaloro)
ticks.constraint: coronary artery disease as treatable only medically
ticks.detail: René Favaloro's development of the coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) in 1967 created a surgical treatment for blocked coronary arteries. A vein harvested from the leg bypasses the obstruction. CABG became the most common open-heart surgery — over 400,000 performed annually in the US. It demonstrably extended millions of lives with coronary disease.

links.label: Google Scholar: Coronary artery bypass surgery (Favaloro)

ticks.name: CT scan (clinical widespread use)
ticks.constraint: imaging limited to flat X-ray shadows of three-dimensional structures
ticks.detail: Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack's CT scanner (first clinical use 1972, widespread by late 1970s) reconstructed three-dimensional cross-sections from multiple X-ray angles. Tumors, strokes, and internal bleeding that X-ray couldn't show became visible. CT scanning revolutionized emergency medicine, oncology, and surgical planning. The 2D X-ray became a 3D diagnostic tool.

links.label: Google Scholar: CT scan (clinical widespread use)

ticks.name: HIV identified / AIDS crisis response
ticks.constraint: retroviruses as medically unimportant human pathogens
ticks.detail: The identification of HIV (Gallo/Montagnier, 1983-1984) and the subsequent development of HIV tests, AZT treatment (1987), combination therapy (1996), and eventually pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP, 2012) tracked medical science's response to a pandemic in real time. AIDS also transformed drug approval processes, patient advocacy in medicine, and the science of antiviral pharmacology.

links.label: Wikipedia: HIV identified / AIDS crisis response
Google Scholar: HIV identified / AIDS crisis response

ticks.name: Viagra / erectile dysfunction treatment
ticks.constraint: male sexual dysfunction as untreatable by pharmacology
ticks.detail: Sildenafil (Viagra) was discovered as a side effect of cardiovascular research. Its 1998 approval demonstrated that sexual function was pharmacologically modifiable — and that a medication could address conditions previously treated as purely psychological. It also launched the era of direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising and changed how openly sexual health is discussed medically.

links.label: Google Scholar: Viagra / erectile dysfunction treatment

ticks.name: Human papillomavirus vaccine (Gardasil)
ticks.constraint: cervical cancer as unpreventable
ticks.detail: The HPV vaccine prevented the leading viral cause of cervical cancer — a cancer killing 300,000 women annually. It was the first vaccine explicitly designed to prevent cancer (rather than preventing infection as a side effect). Cancer prevention through vaccination became a demonstrated reality. The principle is being extended to other cancer-causing viruses.

ticks.name: Liquid biopsy / cancer detection from blood
ticks.constraint: cancer monitoring requiring tumor tissue biopsies
ticks.detail: Circulating tumor DNA in blood can now detect cancer recurrence, monitor treatment response, and screen for early-stage cancer without surgical biopsy. Liquid biopsy companies (GRAIL, Foundation Medicine) promise multi-cancer early detection from a single blood draw. If validated at scale, catching cancers at stage 1 rather than stage 4 would transform oncology outcomes.

links.label: Wikipedia: Liquid biopsy / cancer detection from blood
Google Scholar: Liquid biopsy / cancer detection from blood

ticks.name: Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius / telescope astronomy
ticks.constraint: astronomical knowledge as limited to naked-eye observations of the same sky for 2000 years
ticks.detail: Galileo's Starry Messenger (1610) reported mountains on the Moon, four moons of Jupiter, and thousands of stars invisible to the naked eye. The telescope extended human perception beyond its biological limits for the first time in astronomy. The Milky Way resolved into individual stars. The universe was suddenly, demonstrably, vastly larger than anyone had known.

links.label: Wikipedia: Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius / telescope astronomy
Google Scholar: Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius / telescope astronomy

ticks.name: Newton's calculus / mathematics of change
ticks.constraint: continuous change as undescribable by existing mathematics
ticks.detail: Newton (and independently Leibniz) invented calculus — the mathematics of continuous change. It allowed the calculation of instantaneous velocity, areas under curves, and the behavior of functions at any point. Every physics equation involving rates of change uses calculus. Engineering, economics, statistics, and machine learning all depend on calculus as their mathematical language.

links.label: Wikipedia: Newton's calculus / mathematics of change
Google Scholar: Newton's calculus / mathematics of change

ticks.name: Lavoisier / conservation of mass
ticks.constraint: chemical reactions as transforming the fundamental nature of matter
ticks.detail: Antoine Lavoisier demonstrated that mass is conserved in chemical reactions — matter is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed. This demolished phlogiston theory and established stoichiometry. Modern chemistry's ability to predict and control reactions, design drugs, and engineer materials all depend on conservation of mass as a foundational principle.

links.label: Google Scholar: Lavoisier / conservation of mass

ticks.name: Electromagnetism unified (Faraday/Oersted)
ticks.constraint: electricity and magnetism as independent phenomena
ticks.detail: Faraday's discovery that changing magnetic fields generate electrical currents (1831) completed the electromagnetic unity that Oersted's 1820 discovery had begun. The electric generator, the electric motor, and all electrical power technology depend on electromagnetic induction. Maxwell's later mathematical unification (1865) made the connection theoretical.

ticks.name: Second law of thermodynamics (Clausius/Kelvin)
ticks.constraint: perpetual motion machines as conceivable
ticks.detail: Clausius and Kelvin independently formulated the second law: heat flows from hot to cold, entropy never decreases in a closed system, and perpetual motion is impossible. The universe tends toward disorder. Time has a direction. Every engine efficiency limit, every refrigerator design, every understanding of why aging happens traces to the second law.

links.label: Google Scholar: Second law of thermodynamics (Clausius/Kelvin)

ticks.name: Michelson-Morley experiment / no ether
ticks.constraint: light as requiring a medium (ether) through which to travel
ticks.detail: Michelson and Morley's interferometer found no difference in the speed of light regardless of Earth's direction of travel through the supposed ether. Light didn't need a medium. The ether didn't exist. The result was called 'the most important negative result in physics.' It set the stage for Einstein's special relativity 18 years later.

links.label: Google Scholar: Michelson-Morley experiment / no ether

ticks.name: Einstein's annus mirabilis (four papers)
ticks.constraint: Newtonian mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics as complete and compatible
ticks.detail: In 1905, Einstein published four papers that each transformed physics: the photoelectric effect (quantum theory), Brownian motion (atomic theory), special relativity (space-time), and mass-energy equivalence (E=mc²). Any one would have secured his reputation. Together they define the modern physical worldview. No single year in science's history has been as productive.

links.label: Google Scholar: Einstein's annus mirabilis (four papers)

ticks.name: Superconductivity discovered (Kamerlingh Onnes)
ticks.constraint: electrical resistance as an unavoidable property of conductors at any temperature
ticks.detail: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that mercury's electrical resistance dropped to exactly zero at 4.2 Kelvin. Superconductors have no resistance — current flows forever without energy loss. Applications include MRI magnets, particle accelerator magnets, and potentially lossless power transmission. High-temperature superconductors (1986+) brought the phenomenon closer to practical use.

ticks.name: Nuclear magnetic resonance discovered
ticks.constraint: atomic nuclei as unobservable without disturbing them
ticks.detail: Isidor Rabi's discovery of nuclear magnetic resonance (1938) showed that atomic nuclei, placed in a magnetic field and exposed to radio waves, absorb energy at characteristic frequencies. NMR spectroscopy became chemistry's most powerful analytical tool for determining molecular structure. Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell extended it (1946). Paul Lauterbur's spatial encoding (1973) created MRI.

links.label: Google Scholar: Nuclear magnetic resonance discovered

ticks.name: Solar cell (Bell Labs / practical photovoltaics)
ticks.constraint: solar energy as thermally convertible but not electrically
ticks.detail: Chapin, Fuller, and Pearson's silicon solar cell (1954) converted sunlight to electricity at 6% efficiency — enough to run a radio. Bell Labs' goal was powering remote telephone equipment. The cell was too expensive for general use for 50 years. Solar panel costs have dropped 99.7% since 1977. Solar is now the cheapest source of electricity in history.

links.label: Wikipedia: Solar cell (Bell Labs / practical photovoltaics)
Google Scholar: Solar cell (Bell Labs / practical photovoltaics)

ticks.name: Feynman's 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'
ticks.constraint: manufacturing as limited to top-down machining and chemistry
ticks.detail: Richard Feynman's 1959 lecture proposed building machines atom by atom — bottom-up nanotechnology. He suggested writing the Encyclopedia Britannica on a pinhead and building machines of molecular scale. The lecture launched nanotechnology as a conceptual field 25 years before it became experimentally feasible. Every molecular machine, nanoscale drug delivery system, and quantum dot display traces to Feynman's vision.

links.label: Wikipedia: Feynman's 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'
Google Scholar: Feynman's 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'

ticks.name: Intel 4004 / first commercial microprocessor
ticks.constraint: computing requiring components separately designed for each application
ticks.detail: The 4004 integrated all of a CPU's functions on a single chip — designed for a Japanese calculator company, Busicom, which then sold back the rights to Intel. The general-purpose microprocessor enabled the personal computer, the embedded controller, the modern car (with 100+ microprocessors), and the smartphone. Computing became a commodity ingredient rather than a specialized technology.

links.label: Google Scholar: Intel 4004 / first commercial microprocessor

ticks.name: Altair 8800 / personal computing as hobbyist
ticks.constraint: computers as institutional property requiring professional operation
ticks.detail: The Altair 8800 kit computer (Popular Electronics cover, January 1975) made computing available to individual hobbyists for the first time. Bill Gates and Paul Allen saw the cover and wrote BASIC for it — founding Microsoft. Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs saw the Homebrew Computer Club built around it — founding Apple. The personal computer revolution began in a hobbyist kit.

links.label: Wikipedia: Altair 8800 / personal computing as hobbyist
Google Scholar: Altair 8800 / personal computing as hobbyist

ticks.name: Recombinant insulin / biotech industry born
ticks.constraint: pharmaceutical production as limited to extraction from biological sources
ticks.detail: Genentech's recombinant human insulin (approved 1982, licensed to Eli Lilly) was the first recombinant DNA pharmaceutical product. Previously, insulin came from pig and cow pancreases — a limited, allergenic supply. Recombinant technology produced unlimited, human-identical insulin. It also created the biotechnology industry and the business model of pharma-biotech partnership.

links.label: Wikipedia: Recombinant insulin / biotech industry born
Google Scholar: Recombinant insulin / biotech industry born

ticks.name: Hubble Space Telescope launch
ticks.constraint: astronomical observation as limited by atmospheric distortion
ticks.detail: The Hubble Space Telescope — once its flawed mirror was corrected by the 1993 servicing mission — provided images of unprecedented clarity from above Earth's atmosphere. Its ultra-deep field images revealed galaxies 13 billion light-years away. Hubble's images changed humanity's sense of the universe's scale and age, and enabled precision cosmology.

links.label: Google Scholar: Hubble Space Telescope launch

ticks.name: YouTube launch / video publishing democratized
ticks.constraint: video publishing requiring broadcast infrastructure or physical media
ticks.detail: YouTube's April 2005 launch (first video: 'Me at the Zoo') made video publishing free and global. Within 18 months, Google acquired it for $1.65B. The creator economy, online education (Khan Academy), citizen journalism, and the decline of broadcast television as the primary video medium all trace to YouTube making video a medium anyone could publish in.

links.label: Wikipedia: YouTube launch / video publishing democratized
Google Scholar: YouTube launch / video publishing democratized

ticks.name: Bitcoin whitepaper implemented / blockchain live
ticks.constraint: digital scarcity as impossible without a trusted central authority
ticks.detail: Satoshi Nakamoto's blockchain made digital assets scarce for the first time — each bitcoin can only be spent once, enforced by a distributed ledger. Solving the double-spend problem without a central authority was the tick. Ethereum (2015) extended this to programmable smart contracts. DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, and programmable money follow from the blockchain's ability to create digital scarcity.

links.label: Wikipedia: Bitcoin whitepaper implemented / blockchain live
Google Scholar: Bitcoin whitepaper implemented / blockchain live

ticks.name: Watson wins Jeopardy / NLP crosses human performance
ticks.constraint: natural language question-answering as requiring human-level understanding
ticks.detail: IBM's Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in February 2011. Watson used statistical machine learning on massive text corpora to answer questions requiring inference, wordplay, and broad knowledge. The demonstration was symbolic but real: machine question-answering had crossed a human-level threshold on a well-defined task. AI's public credibility changed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Watson wins Jeopardy / NLP crosses human performance
Google Scholar: Watson wins Jeopardy / NLP crosses human performance

ticks.name: AlphaGo Zero / self-taught superhuman play
ticks.constraint: superhuman game performance requiring human expert knowledge for training
ticks.detail: AlphaGo Zero learned Go entirely through self-play against itself, with no human games as training data — and surpassed all previous AlphaGo versions within days. It discovered moves and strategies that human players had never conceived. The tick: reinforcement learning from self-play could achieve superhuman performance in complex domains without human knowledge as a starting point.

links.label: Wikipedia: AlphaGo Zero / self-taught superhuman play
Google Scholar: AlphaGo Zero / self-taught superhuman play

ticks.name: GPT-2 / language generation crosses coherence threshold
ticks.constraint: machine-generated text as obviously non-human in quality
ticks.detail: OpenAI's GPT-2 generated text coherent enough that OpenAI initially refused to release the full model citing misuse concerns. The debate itself was the tick — it was the first time a language model's output was taken seriously enough to consider withholding. GPT-2 established that scale and training data could produce qualitatively new language capability.

links.label: Wikipedia: GPT-2 / language generation crosses coherence threshold
Google Scholar: GPT-2 / language generation crosses coherence threshold

ticks.name: Codex / GitHub Copilot (code generation)
ticks.constraint: software development requiring a programmer to write every line of code
ticks.detail: OpenAI's Codex model, trained on billions of lines of code, could generate functional code from natural language descriptions. GitHub Copilot (2021) made it available to developers as an AI pair programmer. Productivity gains of 20-55% were documented. The click: programming became less about remembering syntax and more about specifying intent. Non-programmers could produce working code.

links.label: Chen et al. — Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code (2021)

ticks.name: Bronze weapons / military metallurgy
ticks.constraint: weapons as limited to stone, bone, and wood
ticks.detail: Bronze—copper and tin alloyed—produced weapons far harder and sharper than stone while retaining workability. The Bronze Age military balance depended on access to both metals. Armies with bronze weapons dominated those without. The metallurgical arms race that began with bronze runs through iron, steel, aluminum, titanium, and carbon fiber.

links.label: Google Scholar: Bronze weapons / military metallurgy

ticks.name: Battle of Marathon / citizen-soldier victory
ticks.constraint: professional or mercenary armies as necessarily superior to citizen soldiers
ticks.detail: Ten thousand Athenian citizen hoplites defeated a Persian army twice their size at Marathon. The victory established that motivated citizens, fighting for their own city, could defeat professional imperial armies. The civic-military connection — the idea that political freedom produces military effectiveness — shaped Western military thought for 2,500 years.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Marathon / citizen-soldier victory
Google Scholar: Battle of Marathon / citizen-soldier victory

ticks.name: Alexander's siege of Tyre / naval and siege warfare
ticks.constraint: island cities as impregnable to land-based armies
ticks.detail: Alexander the Great besieged Tyre — an island fortress — for seven months by building a causeway from the mainland. He combined naval blockade, siege towers, and engineering to take what everyone assumed was safe. The siege established that no position is truly impregnable given sufficient engineering resources and political will.

links.label: Wikipedia: Alexander's siege of Tyre / naval and siege warfare
Google Scholar: Alexander's siege of Tyre / naval and siege warfare

ticks.name: Hannibal crosses the Alps / strategic surprise
ticks.constraint: Alpine mountain ranges as an impassable barrier to military movement
ticks.detail: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with 37 elephants and 50,000 troops achieved total strategic surprise. Three subsequent victories (Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae) nearly destroyed Rome. Cannae (216 BC) — where Hannibal encircled a larger Roman army — remains the paradigmatic example of operational encirclement studied at military academies worldwide.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hannibal crosses the Alps / strategic surprise
Google Scholar: Hannibal crosses the Alps / strategic surprise

ticks.name: Caesar's Gallic Wars / total conquest doctrine
ticks.constraint: conquest as requiring the submission of ruling elites only
ticks.detail: Caesar's conquest of Gaul (58-50 BC) killed approximately 1 million Gauls and enslaved another million — roughly a third of the total population. The deliberate destruction of the population's capacity to resist, not just its military forces, was systematic. Caesar's Commentarii documented the doctrine that would be called 'total war' in its modern form.

links.label: Wikipedia: Caesar's Gallic Wars / total conquest doctrine
Google Scholar: Caesar's Gallic Wars / total conquest doctrine

ticks.name: Battle of Teutoburg Forest / limits of Roman expansion
ticks.constraint: Roman military superiority as unlimited in any terrain
ticks.detail: Germanic tribes under Arminius ambushed three Roman legions (17,000 men) in the Teutoburg Forest and annihilated them. Rome never again seriously attempted to conquer Germania. The Teutoburg Forest established that military superiority is terrain-dependent — the Roman legion optimized for open terrain was vulnerable to ambush in forests. Asymmetric warfare against a superior conventional force begins here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Teutoburg Forest / limits of Roman expansion
Google Scholar: Battle of Teutoburg Forest / limits of Roman expansion

ticks.name: Mongol invasions / mobile warfare doctrine
ticks.constraint: cavalry armies as limited to raiding and harassment
ticks.detail: The Mongol Empire's military system — extreme mobility, feigned retreats, coordinated multi-column attacks, psychological warfare, and siege engineer experts — defeated every army it faced for 50 years. The Mongol system showed that mobile cavalry could conduct sustained campaigns over thousands of miles and defeat much larger sedentary armies. At their peak, they controlled more territory than any empire in history.

links.label: Wikipedia: Mongol invasions / mobile warfare doctrine
Google Scholar: Mongol invasions / mobile warfare doctrine

ticks.name: Agincourt / longbow defeats armored cavalry
ticks.constraint: the armored knight as the decisive military instrument of medieval Europe
ticks.detail: At Agincourt, 6,000 English (mostly longbowmen) defeated 20,000 French including the flower of French nobility. English longbow arrows penetrating plate armor at short range, combined with the mud that slowed the French advance, produced a slaughter. The medieval military aristocracy's military dominance ended here. The feudal social order it supported began its long decline.

links.label: Wikipedia: Agincourt / longbow defeats armored cavalry
Google Scholar: Agincourt / longbow defeats armored cavalry

ticks.name: Battle of Lepanto / end of Ottoman naval dominance
ticks.constraint: Ottoman naval power as unchallengeable in the Mediterranean
ticks.detail: The Holy League's fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto — the largest naval battle since Actium. Over 200 Ottoman galleys were destroyed. The battle checked Ottoman western expansion and ended the perception of Ottoman invincibility. It also demonstrated that the galley's era was ending — galleons with broadside artillery were the future.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Lepanto / end of Ottoman naval dominance
Google Scholar: Battle of Lepanto / end of Ottoman naval dominance

ticks.name: Thirty Years' War / religious vs. political warfare
ticks.constraint: European warfare as primarily dynastic or religious in motivation
ticks.detail: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began as a religious war and ended as a political one — by 1635, France (Catholic) was supporting Protestant states against the Catholic Habsburgs because the strategic balance mattered more than religion. The Peace of Westphalia that ended it established state sovereignty and religious tolerance as the organizing principles of European order.

links.label: Wikipedia: Thirty Years' War / religious vs. political warfare
Google Scholar: Thirty Years' War / religious vs. political warfare

ticks.name: Frederick the Great's oblique order / tactical geometry
ticks.constraint: linear battlefield tactics as static and symmetrical
ticks.detail: Frederick the Great's oblique order — advancing one wing of the army at an angle while holding the other back — allowed smaller Prussian armies to defeat larger opponents by concentrating force on one flank before the enemy could respond. Prussian drill and discipline made this executable in battle. The idea that tactics could be analyzed geometrically influenced military theory through WWI.

links.label: Wikipedia: Frederick the Great's oblique order / tactical geometry
Google Scholar: Frederick the Great's oblique order / tactical geometry

ticks.name: Napoleon's defeat / logistics and overextension
ticks.constraint: military genius as capable of overcoming strategic overextension
ticks.detail: The Russian campaign (1812) and subsequent campaigns showed that even Napoleon's operational genius couldn't overcome the strategic reality that an army operating 1,000 miles from its supply base, in Russian winter, against an opponent willing to trade territory for time, was doomed. The limits of operational genius against strategic geography is Napoleon's lesson.

links.label: Wikipedia: Napoleon's defeat / logistics and overextension
Google Scholar: Napoleon's defeat / logistics and overextension

ticks.name: Monitor vs. Virginia / end of wooden warships
ticks.constraint: wooden warships as the dominant naval technology
ticks.detail: The ironclad duel at Hampton Roads (1862) made every wooden warship in every navy on Earth obsolete within days of the engagement. Britain immediately began converting its fleet. The naval arms race that followed — Britain vs. France, then Britain vs. Germany — produced the Dreadnought and eventually contributed to the conditions for WWI.

links.label: Wikipedia: Monitor vs. Virginia / end of wooden warships
Google Scholar: Monitor vs. Virginia / end of wooden warships

ticks.name: Schlieffen Plan failure / war becomes attritional
ticks.constraint: the assumption that a modern industrial war could be short
ticks.detail: Germany's Schlieffen Plan assumed France could be knocked out in six weeks before Russia mobilized. It failed at the Marne. Both sides dug trenches. For four years, industrial nations threw resources into a deadlocked front. The lesson that industrial war between roughly equal powers tends toward attrition — and that attrition favors the side with more resources — shaped all subsequent strategic planning.

links.label: Wikipedia: Schlieffen Plan failure / war becomes attritional
Google Scholar: Schlieffen Plan failure / war becomes attritional

ticks.name: Stormtrooper tactics / infiltration assault
ticks.constraint: trench warfare deadlock as militarily insoluble
ticks.detail: German Stormtrooper (Sturmtruppen) infiltration tactics in 1918 — small groups bypassing strong points, penetrating deep into rear areas, disrupting command and supply — broke the Western Front's tactical deadlock. The German Spring Offensive (1918) advanced further in days than years of previous combat had managed. The method influenced blitzkrieg, modern special operations, and counterinsurgency.

links.label: Google Scholar: Stormtrooper tactics / infiltration assault

ticks.name: V-2 rocket / ballistic missile warfare
ticks.constraint: aerial attack as requiring manned aircraft
ticks.detail: The V-2 was the world's first ballistic missile — it flew to the edge of space and fell unpredictably on London from 300 miles away. No defense was possible. Wernher von Braun's team that built it was captured by the Americans and became the core of NASA. The V-2 directly begat the ICBM, the space race, and the satellite — the most consequential weapons program's civilian legacy.

links.label: Wikipedia: V-2 rocket / ballistic missile warfare
Google Scholar: V-2 rocket / ballistic missile warfare

ticks.name: Hiroshima and Nagasaki / nuclear warfare reality
ticks.constraint: the absolute destruction of a city as requiring months of conventional bombing
ticks.detail: A single aircraft, a single bomb, a city gone. Hiroshima (August 6) and Nagasaki (August 9) demonstrated that nuclear weapons were not just more powerful bombs but qualitatively different instruments. Japan's surrender within days ended the Pacific War. The shadow of August 1945 has governed every great-power calculation about war ever since.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hiroshima and Nagasaki / nuclear warfare reality
Google Scholar: Hiroshima and Nagasaki / nuclear warfare reality

ticks.name: U-2 incident / aerial reconnaissance satellites
ticks.constraint: strategic intelligence as requiring risky human infiltration
ticks.detail: The U-2 spy plane shot down over the USSR (1960) exposed American aerial reconnaissance, creating a diplomatic crisis. The solution: reconnaissance satellites, which orbit above airspace rights, provided intelligence without violating sovereignty. The Corona satellite program (1960) photographed the USSR with impunity. Every military satellite — GPS, signals intelligence, imagery — traces to this transition.

links.label: Wikipedia: U-2 incident / aerial reconnaissance satellites
Google Scholar: U-2 incident / aerial reconnaissance satellites

ticks.name: Tet Offensive / information warfare and public opinion
ticks.constraint: military success as determinative of war's outcome regardless of political will
ticks.detail: The Tet Offensive (1968) was a military failure for North Vietnam — most objectives were quickly retaken. But Walter Cronkite's assessment that the war was a stalemate, broadcast to 27 million Americans, destroyed public confidence in the Johnson administration's optimism. Tet demonstrated that in a democracy, the information war can be more decisive than the military war.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tet Offensive / information warfare and public opinion
Google Scholar: Tet Offensive / information warfare and public opinion

ticks.name: Falklands War / precision strike lessons
ticks.constraint: surface ships as protected against missile attack by point-defense systems
ticks.detail: Argentine Exocet missiles sinking British ships demonstrated that ship-launched and air-launched anti-ship missiles had outpaced naval defensive systems. The lesson: surface ships are vulnerable to precision strike and must operate with layered air defense. Every naval doctrine revision since 1982 addresses the Falklands lesson about precision anti-ship weapons.

links.label: Wikipedia: Falklands War / precision strike lessons
Google Scholar: Falklands War / precision strike lessons

ticks.name: Iraq War / shock and awe doctrine
ticks.constraint: rapid military victory as insufficient without post-conflict planning
ticks.detail: Operation Iraqi Freedom achieved military objectives in 21 days. The subsequent insurgency lasted years. The lesson — that rapid military victory without political consolidation produces strategic failure — has been called 'the Iraq syndrome.' Military operations must integrate governance, reconstruction, and political legitimacy from day one. Every subsequent COIN doctrine reflects this.

links.label: Wikipedia: Iraq War / shock and awe doctrine
Google Scholar: Iraq War / shock and awe doctrine

ticks.name: VOC / first multinational corporation
ticks.constraint: commercial ventures as bounded by the capital of individual merchants
ticks.detail: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was the first company to issue tradeable shares to the public, pay dividends, maintain a permanent standing organization, and operate across continents. It had its own army and navy, could declare war, and governed territories. The multinational corporation — the dominant organizational form of global capitalism — begins here.

links.label: Google Scholar: VOC / first multinational corporation

ticks.name: South Sea Bubble / speculation and crash
ticks.constraint: share price as tethered to underlying business value even loosely
ticks.detail: The South Sea Company's stock rose 10x in months based on anticipated monopoly profits from trading with South America — profits that never materialized. The crash wiped out thousands of investors, including Isaac Newton, who reportedly said 'I can calculate the movement of stars, but not the madness of men.' The bubble established that financial mania and crash are recurring features of market economies.

links.label: Wikipedia: South Sea Bubble / speculation and crash
Google Scholar: South Sea Bubble / speculation and crash

ticks.name: Corn Laws debate / free trade vs. protection
ticks.constraint: trade policy as obviously favorable to domestic producers
ticks.detail: The Corn Laws (1815) protected British landowners by taxing grain imports. Ricardo's comparative advantage argument and the Anti-Corn Law League's campaign produced their repeal in 1846. The Corn Law debate established free trade as an economic doctrine, Cobden and Bright as its political champions, and the tension between producer and consumer interests as the permanent fault line of trade policy.

links.label: Wikipedia: Corn Laws debate / free trade vs. protection
Google Scholar: Corn Laws debate / free trade vs. protection

ticks.name: Telegraph and financial markets
ticks.constraint: price information as limited to the speed of physical transport
ticks.detail: The telegraph (1844) allowed price information to travel faster than goods. For the first time, commodity prices in New York and Chicago could converge — arbitrage opportunities disappeared in seconds rather than days. Financial markets became integrated across geography. Reuters (1851) built its news agency on telegraph arbitrage information. Real-time global financial markets begin with the telegraph.

links.label: Google Scholar: Telegraph and financial markets

ticks.name: Das Kapital (Marx) / critique of capitalism
ticks.constraint: capitalism as a natural or eternal economic arrangement
ticks.detail: Marx's analysis of capitalism as a historically specific mode of production — with its own internal contradictions (falling rate of profit, capital concentration, class conflict) that would produce its own supersession — provided the most systematic critique of capitalist economics ever written. Whether or not one accepts his conclusions, every subsequent economics engages with his framework.

links.label: Wikipedia: Das Kapital (Marx) / critique of capitalism
Google Scholar: Das Kapital (Marx) / critique of capitalism

ticks.name: Sherman Antitrust Act / competition law
ticks.constraint: monopoly power as a market outcome requiring no legal remedy
ticks.detail: The Sherman Act (1890) established that combinations in restraint of trade were illegal — that market dominance achieved through predatory means violated the public interest. Standard Oil, AT&T, and Microsoft were all eventually broken up or constrained under antitrust. Competition policy as an ongoing regulatory function begins here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Sherman Antitrust Act / competition law
Google Scholar: Sherman Antitrust Act / competition law

ticks.name: Federal Reserve Act / US central banking
ticks.constraint: US financial panics as manageable only through J.P. Morgan's personal intervention
ticks.detail: After the Panic of 1907 required JP Morgan to personally organize the banking system's rescue, Congress created the Federal Reserve. The Fed's ability to provide emergency liquidity — the lender of last resort function — prevented panics from cascading into depressions. The 2008 crisis demonstrated both the Fed's power and its limits.

links.label: Wikipedia: Federal Reserve Act / US central banking
Google Scholar: Federal Reserve Act / US central banking

ticks.name: Glass-Steagall Act / banking separation
ticks.constraint: commercial banks' ability to gamble depositors' money in securities markets
ticks.detail: The Glass-Steagall Act (1933) separated commercial banking (deposits, loans) from investment banking (securities underwriting). It created the FDIC (deposit insurance). For 60 years, it prevented bank runs by guaranteeing deposits. Its repeal (1999) is credited by some with contributing to the 2008 financial crisis. The tension between financial integration and stability continues.

links.label: Google Scholar: Glass-Steagall Act / banking separation

ticks.name: Bretton Woods / dollar as world reserve currency
ticks.constraint: international trade as requiring bilateral currency negotiations
ticks.detail: The 1944 conference established the US dollar (pegged to gold at $35/oz) as the world reserve currency. All other currencies were pegged to the dollar. The IMF and World Bank were created to manage the system. When Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971, the dollar remained the reserve currency despite no longer being gold-backed — pure US geopolitical and economic dominance.

links.label: Wikipedia: Bretton Woods / dollar as world reserve currency
Google Scholar: Bretton Woods / dollar as world reserve currency

ticks.name: Floating exchange rates / end of Bretton Woods
ticks.constraint: currency exchange rates as fixed by international agreement
ticks.detail: Nixon's closing of the gold window ended fixed exchange rates. Currencies now float against each other, set by market supply and demand. Currency markets became the world's largest financial markets ($7 trillion daily turnover). Exchange rate volatility became a new source of business risk and speculation. The IMF's purpose was partially made obsolete overnight.

links.label: Wikipedia: Floating exchange rates / end of Bretton Woods
Google Scholar: Floating exchange rates / end of Bretton Woods

ticks.name: Index funds (Vanguard) / passive investing
ticks.constraint: investment success as requiring active stock-picking skill
ticks.detail: John Bogle founded Vanguard and launched the first index mutual fund (1976). The idea: if most active managers underperform the market after fees, why not own the whole market at minimal cost? Index funds have grown from a curiosity to managing $15+ trillion — more than half of all US equity fund assets. The active management industry's economics have been permanently disrupted.

links.label: Google Scholar: Index funds (Vanguard) / passive investing

ticks.name: Big Bang / financial deregulation (London)
ticks.constraint: London's Stock Exchange as a gentlemen's club with fixed commissions
ticks.detail: Margaret Thatcher's 'Big Bang' (October 27, 1986) deregulated London's financial markets — abolishing fixed commissions, allowing foreign ownership of brokers, and introducing electronic trading. London competed with New York for global financial dominance. Financial services grew to dominate the UK economy. The template for financial deregulation that preceded the 2008 crisis.

links.label: Google Scholar: Big Bang / financial deregulation (London)

ticks.name: NAFTA / regional free trade
ticks.constraint: hemispheric trade as managed through bilateral tariff negotiations
ticks.detail: NAFTA created a trilateral free trade zone encompassing 450 million people and $19 trillion in GDP. Manufacturing supply chains integrated across North America. Mexico became a major US manufacturing partner. NAFTA's distributional effects — job losses in US manufacturing, agricultural disruption in Mexico — fueled the populist backlash that produced Trump's 2016 victory and USMCA renegotiation.

links.label: Google Scholar: NAFTA / regional free trade

ticks.name: Microfinance / Grameen Bank model global spread
ticks.constraint: small-scale entrepreneurship in developing countries as requiring conventional bank credit
ticks.detail: Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank (founded 1983, Nobel Peace Prize 2006) demonstrated that small loans to poor women — with peer group accountability replacing collateral — could generate repayment rates exceeding conventional banking. Microfinance spread globally. Its impact is contested — later research showed mixed effects on poverty reduction — but it fundamentally changed development economics.

links.label: Wikipedia: Microfinance / Grameen Bank model global spread
Google Scholar: Microfinance / Grameen Bank model global spread

ticks.name: Global financial crisis / shadow banking collapse
ticks.constraint: mortgage risk as diversified away through securitization
ticks.detail: The creation of mortgage-backed securities, CDOs, and CDO-squareds distributed subprime mortgage risk throughout the global financial system — and then concentrated it in institutions that hadn't disclosed their exposure. When housing prices fell, the entire chain collapsed. Lehman Brothers' failure triggered a global credit freeze. The $700B TARP bailout and Fed intervention prevented another Great Depression.

links.label: Wikipedia: Global financial crisis / shadow banking collapse
Google Scholar: Global financial crisis / shadow banking collapse

ticks.name: Sharing economy / Uber and Airbnb
ticks.constraint: asset utilization requiring ownership by the service provider
ticks.detail: Airbnb (2008) and Uber (2009) demonstrated that underutilized private assets — spare bedrooms, personal cars — could be economically deployed through a platform matching supply with demand. The sharing economy created a new economic sector worth hundreds of billions and disrupted hotels and taxis globally. It also created new regulatory challenges around labor classification and safety.

links.label: Wikipedia: Sharing economy / Uber and Airbnb
Google Scholar: Sharing economy / Uber and Airbnb

ticks.name: ICO boom / cryptocurrency fundraising
ticks.constraint: startup fundraising as requiring accredited investors or IPO infrastructure
ticks.detail: Initial Coin Offerings raised $5.6B in 2017 by selling cryptocurrency tokens directly to the public without SEC registration. It democratized startup funding — and also enabled massive fraud. The SEC's subsequent enforcement actions established that most ICOs were unregistered securities. The episode revealed how existing financial regulation struggled to address cryptographic assets.

links.label: Google Scholar: ICO boom / cryptocurrency fundraising

ticks.name: COVID pandemic / remote work as default
ticks.constraint: knowledge work as requiring physical co-location in offices
ticks.detail: The COVID-19 pandemic forced the largest work-from-home experiment in history — 45% of US workers shifted to remote work in spring 2020. Zoom, Slack, and remote collaboration tools became essential infrastructure. The experiment proved that much knowledge work could be done remotely without productivity collapse. The geography of work and commercial real estate were permanently changed.

links.label: Wikipedia: COVID pandemic / remote work as default
Google Scholar: COVID pandemic / remote work as default

ticks.name: Avicenna's floating man / pure self-awareness
ticks.constraint: self-knowledge as requiring sensory or bodily experience
ticks.detail: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) proposed a thought experiment: imagine a person floating in air, senses blocked, unable to feel their own body. They would still be aware that they exist. This anticipates Descartes' cogito by 600 years — and locates self-awareness in pure mental existence, independent of body. Islamic philosophy's contribution to epistemology is systematically underappreciated.

links.label: Wikipedia: Avicenna's floating man / pure self-awareness
Google Scholar: Avicenna's floating man / pure self-awareness

ticks.name: Aquinas' synthesis / faith and reason
ticks.constraint: Christian theology and Aristotelian philosophy as incompatible
ticks.detail: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica synthesized Aristotle's philosophical system with Christian theology — showing that reason and faith are complementary, not opposed. Natural theology (proving God's existence through reason) and systematic theology (elaborating revealed doctrine) were both legitimate intellectual enterprises. Thomism became Catholic philosophy's official framework and remains so.

links.label: Wikipedia: Aquinas' synthesis / faith and reason
Google Scholar: Aquinas' synthesis / faith and reason

ticks.name: Francis Bacon / inductive method
ticks.constraint: natural knowledge as derivable from first principles through deduction
ticks.detail: Bacon's Novum Organum proposed induction — systematic collection of observations and generalization — as the method of natural philosophy. Knowledge should rise from particulars to generals, not descend from assumed generals. Bacon founded the empiricist tradition in philosophy and the Royal Society's experimental program. The tension between induction (Bacon) and deduction (Descartes) structures modern epistemology.

links.label: Google Scholar: Francis Bacon / inductive method

ticks.name: Locke's Essay on Human Understanding / tabula rasa
ticks.constraint: innate ideas as the source of human knowledge
ticks.detail: Locke argued the mind at birth is a blank slate (tabula rasa) — all knowledge comes from experience, either sensation or reflection. Against Descartes' innate ideas and rationalism. Locke's empiricism, continued by Berkeley and Hume, became the dominant philosophical tradition in English-speaking philosophy. The nature-nurture debate originates here.

links.label: Wikipedia: Locke's Essay on Human Understanding / tabula rasa
Google Scholar: Locke's Essay on Human Understanding / tabula rasa

ticks.name: Berkeley / idealism (esse est percipi)
ticks.constraint: the material world as existing independently of minds
ticks.detail: George Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived' — objects exist only as ideas in minds. There is no mind-independent material world. This idealist position was designed to defeat skepticism (you can't doubt that you have experiences) while preserving common sense. Kant partially responded to Berkeley. The debate between idealism, realism, and pragmatism about the nature of reality continues.

links.label: Google Scholar: Berkeley / idealism (esse est percipi)

ticks.name: Hume's problem of induction
ticks.constraint: inductive reasoning as philosophically justified
ticks.detail: Hume pointed out that induction — inferring a general principle from particular observations — cannot be logically justified. No amount of past experience logically guarantees future regularity. The sun has always risen, but there's no logical proof it must rise tomorrow. This 'problem of induction' has never been solved. Popper's falsificationism and Bayesian probability are the best responses.

links.label: Google Scholar: Hume's problem of induction

ticks.name: Kant's Groundwork / categorical imperative
ticks.constraint: moral philosophy as based on consequences or divine command
ticks.detail: Kant's categorical imperative — act only according to rules you could will to become universal laws — provided a reason-based alternative to both consequentialism and divine command ethics. You could derive moral obligations from pure reason, regardless of desire or consequences. Kantian deontology remains one of ethics' two main frameworks (alongside consequentialism).

links.label: Google Scholar: Kant's Groundwork / categorical imperative

ticks.name: Kierkegaard / existential anxiety and choice
ticks.constraint: philosophy as addressing universal reason rather than individual existence
ticks.detail: Søren Kierkegaard wrote under pseudonyms to enact the subjective perspective he was philosophizing about. The 'stages' of existence (aesthetic, ethical, religious) required genuine personal choice, not rational demonstration. The anxiety of freedom — that we must choose without guarantee — is the fundamental human condition. Kierkegaard founded existentialism and influenced Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus.

links.label: Wikipedia: Kierkegaard / existential anxiety and choice
Google Scholar: Kierkegaard / existential anxiety and choice

ticks.name: Mill's On the Subjection of Women
ticks.constraint: women's legal and social inequality as natural or inevitable
ticks.detail: John Stuart Mill's argument that women's inequality was the product of custom and law, not nature, and that equality would benefit both women and society, was the most rigorous philosophical defense of women's rights before the suffrage movement. Mill connected liberal political philosophy's premises to feminist conclusions — you cannot consistently believe in liberty while denying it to half the population.

links.label: Wikipedia: Mill's On the Subjection of Women
Google Scholar: Mill's On the Subjection of Women

ticks.name: Logical positivism / Vienna Circle
ticks.constraint: metaphysics as a legitimate philosophical enterprise
ticks.detail: The Vienna Circle's logical positivism (Schlick, Carnap, Neurath) held that only empirically verifiable statements or logical tautologies were meaningful — all other philosophical statements were literally nonsensical. Most of traditional metaphysics was dismissed. The verification principle collapsed under its own weight (itself unverifiable), but logical positivism permanently shaped analytic philosophy's scientific orientation.

links.label: Google Scholar: Logical positivism / Vienna Circle

ticks.name: Popper's falsificationism / philosophy of science
ticks.constraint: scientific theories as verified by confirming evidence
ticks.detail: Karl Popper proposed that science advances not by confirming theories but by trying to falsify them — a genuinely scientific theory must make predictions that could be proven wrong. Freudian psychoanalysis and Marxism, he argued, were unfalsifiable and therefore not science. Falsificationism defined the 'demarcation problem' and shaped how scientists talk about what science is and isn't.

links.label: Wikipedia: Popper's falsificationism / philosophy of science
Google Scholar: Popper's falsificationism / philosophy of science

ticks.name: Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions
ticks.constraint: science as cumulative progress toward truth
ticks.detail: Thomas Kuhn's paradigm shift — normal science works within an established framework until anomalies accumulate and a revolution replaces the paradigm — challenged the linear, cumulative view of scientific progress. Science is sociological as well as logical. 'Paradigm shift' entered common language. Kuhn's analysis of how revolutionary science actually works changed philosophy of science, science studies, and how scientists understand their own activity.
